topics.title: Reference Formulas for Chapter 1
topics.preamble: The following relations are used repeatedly throughout this chapter. They should be memorised, since the formula sheet supplied in the examination contains only the divergence, gradient, curl and Laplacian operators — not the coordinate transformations. **(A) Cartesian ↔ Cylindrical — point transformation** $$ \rho = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}},\qquad \phi = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{y}{x},\qquad z = z $$ $$ x = \rho\cos\phi,\qquad y = \rho\sin\phi,\qquad z = z $$ **(B) Cartesian → Cylindrical — vector components** $$ A_{\rho} = A_{x}\cos\phi + A_{y}\sin\phi $$ $$ A_{\phi} = -A_{x}\sin\phi + A_{y}\cos\phi $$ $$ A_{z} = A_{z} $$ **(C) Cylindrical → Cartesian — vector components** $$ A_{x} = A_{\rho}\cos\phi - A_{\phi}\sin\phi $$ $$ A_{y} = A_{\rho}\sin\phi + A_{\phi}\cos\phi $$ $$ A_{z} = A_{z} $$ **(D) Cartesian ↔ Spherical — point transformation** $$ r = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}},\qquad \theta = \cos^{-1}\!\frac{z}{r} = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}}{z},\qquad \phi = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{y}{x} $$ $$ x = r\sin\theta\cos\phi,\qquad y = r\sin\theta\sin\phi,\qquad z = r\cos\theta $$ **(E) Cartesian → Spherical — vector components** $$ A_{r} = A_{x}\sin\theta\cos\phi + A_{y}\sin\theta\sin\phi + A_{z}\cos\theta $$ $$ A_{\theta} = A_{x}\cos\theta\cos\phi + A_{y}\cos\theta\sin\phi - A_{z}\sin\theta $$ $$ A_{\phi} = -A_{x}\sin\phi + A_{y}\cos\phi $$ **(F) Cylindrical → Spherical — unit vector relations** $$ \hat{a}_{\rho} = \sin\theta\,\hat{a}_{r} + \cos\theta\,\hat{a}_{\theta} $$ $$ \hat{a}_{z} = \cos\theta\,\hat{a}_{r} - \sin\theta\,\hat{a}_{\theta} $$ $$ \hat{a}_{\phi} = \hat{a}_{\phi},\qquad z = r\cos\theta $$ **(G) Quadrant rule for $\phi$ — the most common source of error** The calculator’s $\tan^{-1}$ returns a value only in $(-90^{\circ},+90^{\circ})$. Always fix the quadrant from the signs of $x$ and $y$: | Quadrant | Signs | Correction | Range | |---|---|---|---| | I | $x>0$, $y>0$ | $\phi=\tan^{-1}\|y/x\|$ | $0^{\circ}$–$90^{\circ}$ | | II | $x<0$, $y>0$ | $\phi=180^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\|y/x\|$ | $90^{\circ}$–$180^{\circ}$ | | III | $x<0$, $y<0$ | $\phi=180^{\circ}+\tan^{-1}\|y/x\|$ | $180^{\circ}$–$270^{\circ}$ | | IV | $x>0$, $y<0$ | $\phi=360^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\|y/x\|$ | $270^{\circ}$–$360^{\circ}$ | Useful shortcut: once $\rho$ is known, $\cos\phi = x/\rho$ and $\sin\phi = y/\rho$ directly — no quadrant ambiguity arises. This is used throughout the solutions below. **(H) Differential elements — line, surface and volume** | System | Line $d\mathbf{l}$ | Surface $d\mathbf{S}$ (constant-coordinate faces) | Volume $dv$ | |---|---|---|---| | Cartesian | $dx\,\hat{a}_{x}+dy\,\hat{a}_{y}+dz\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $dy\,dz\,\hat{a}_{x}$; $dx\,dz\,\hat{a}_{y}$; $dx\,dy\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $dx\,dy\,dz$ | | Cylindrical | $d\rho\,\hat{a}_{\rho}+\rho\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi}+dz\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $\rho\,d\phi\,dz\,\hat{a}_{\rho}$; $d\rho\,dz\,\hat{a}_{\phi}$; $\rho\,d\rho\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $\rho\,d\rho\,d\phi\,dz$ | | Spherical | $dr\,\hat{a}_{r}+r\,d\theta\,\hat{a}_{\theta}+r\sin\theta\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi}$ | $r^{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{r}$; $r\sin\theta\,dr\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{\theta}$; $r\,dr\,d\theta\,\hat{a}_{\phi}$ | $r^{2}\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi$ |

topics.examDefinition: A field assigns a value to every point in space. A scalar field (temperature, potential $V$) has magnitude only; a vector field (force, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{H}$) has magnitude and direction. Electromagnetics is built on scalar potentials and vector field intensities. Unit vectors $\mathbf{a}_{x}$, $\mathbf{a}_{y}$, $\mathbf{a}_{z}$ (or $\mathbf{a}_{\rho}$, $\mathbf{a}_{\phi}$, $\mathbf{a}_{r}$, $\mathbf{a}_{\theta}$) give direction.

topics.title: Reference Formulas for Chapter 2
topics.preamble: **(A) Physical constants** $$ \varepsilon_{0} = 8.854\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m},\qquad \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 9\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{m/F},\qquad \frac{1}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 1.7975\times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m/F} $$ **(B) Coulomb’s law and the field of a point charge** $$ \mathbf{F}_{12} = \frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}\,\hat{a}_{R_{12}},\qquad \mathbf{E} = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}\,\hat{a}_{R},\qquad \mathbf{D} = \varepsilon_{0}\mathbf{E} = \frac{Q}{4\pi R^{2}}\,\hat{a}_{R} $$ where $\mathbf{R}$ is the vector from the charge to the field point and $\hat{a}_{R} = \mathbf{R}/|\mathbf{R}|$. **(C) Standard charge configurations (results derived in this chapter)** | Configuration | $\mathbf{E}$ | Notes | |---|---|---| | Point charge $Q$ | $\displaystyle\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}\,\hat{a}_{R}$ | $R$ = distance charge → point | | Infinite line charge $\rho_{L}$ | $\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}\rho}\,\hat{a}_{\rho}$ | $\rho$ = perpendicular distance from the line | | Infinite sheet charge $\rho_{S}$ | $\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\,\hat{a}_{N}$ | independent of distance; $\hat{a}_{N}$ points from the sheet toward the field point | **(D) Gauss’s law** $$ \oint_{S}\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = Q_{\mathrm{enc}} \quad\text{(integral form)},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{D} = \rho_{v} \quad\text{(point form)} $$ **(E) The three golden rules for superposition problems** 1. **Direction first.** For each source, find the unit vector pointing from the source to the field point. Nearly all lost marks come from a wrong sign here. 2. **For a line charge, use the perpendicular distance.** If the line is parallel to the $x$-axis, the coordinate $x$ of the field point is irrelevant — only the $(y,z)$ offsets matter. Likewise for lines parallel to $y$ or $z$. 3. **For a sheet charge, only the side matters.** The magnitude $\rho_{S}/(2\varepsilon_{0})$ is the same everywhere; only the sign of $\hat{a}_{N}$ changes depending on which side of the sheet the field point lies. **(F) Divergence operator (supplied on the examination formula sheet)** $$ \begin{aligned} \text{Cartesian:}&\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{D} = \frac{\partial D_{x}}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial D_{y}}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial D_{z}}{\partial z}\\[4pt] \text{Cylindrical:}&\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{D} = \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial(\rho D_{\rho})}{\partial\rho} +\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial D_{\phi}}{\partial\phi} +\frac{\partial D_{z}}{\partial z}\\[4pt] \text{Spherical:}&\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{D} = \frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial(r^{2}D_{r})}{\partial r} +\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial(D_{\theta}\sin\theta)}{\partial\theta} +\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial D_{\phi}}{\partial\phi} \end{aligned} $$ **(G) Divergence theorem** $$ \oint_{S}\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_{v}(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D})\,dv $$ It converts a closed surface integral into a volume integral over the enclosed volume. **(H) Differential elements — essential for the integrals** | System | Line $d\mathbf{l}$ | Surface $d\mathbf{S}$ (constant-coordinate faces) | Volume $dv$ | |---|---|---|---| | Cartesian | $dx\,\hat{a}_{x}+dy\,\hat{a}_{y}+dz\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $dy\,dz\,\hat{a}_{x}$; $dx\,dz\,\hat{a}_{y}$; $dx\,dy\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $dx\,dy\,dz$ | | Cylindrical | $d\rho\,\hat{a}_{\rho}+\rho\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi}+dz\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $\rho\,d\phi\,dz\,\hat{a}_{\rho}$; $d\rho\,dz\,\hat{a}_{\phi}$; $\rho\,d\rho\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $\rho\,d\rho\,d\phi\,dz$ | | Spherical | $dr\,\hat{a}_{r}+r\,d\theta\,\hat{a}_{\theta}+r\sin\theta\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi}$ | $r^{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{r}$; $r\sin\theta\,dr\,d\phi\,\hat{a}_{\theta}$; $r\,dr\,d\theta\,\hat{a}_{\phi}$ | $r^{2}\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi$ | **(I) Standard integrals used repeatedly** $$ \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}\phi\,d\phi = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2}\phi\,d\phi = \frac{\pi}{4},\qquad \int\sin^{2}\phi\,d\phi = \frac{\phi}{2}-\frac{\sin 2\phi}{4} $$ $$ \int\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\sin^{2}\theta \quad\text{(or equivalently }\tfrac{1}{2}\text{ over }0\to\pi/2\text{)}, \qquad \int\sin 2\theta\,d\theta = -\tfrac{1}{2}\cos 2\theta $$ **Method note.** On each face of the closed surface, the outward normal is $+\hat{a}_{u}$ on the face of larger coordinate $u$ and $-\hat{a}_{u}$ on the face of smaller coordinate $u$. Getting these six signs right is the whole problem.

topics.examDefinition: Coulomb’s law gives the force between two point charges in free space (or a linear dielectric if $\varepsilon$ replaces $\varepsilon_{0}$). Force is repulsive for like charges and attractive for opposite charges, and acts along the line joining the charges. It is the starting point for defining $\mathbf{E}$.

topics.examDefinition: Divergence at a point is the outward flux per unit volume as the volume shrinks to that point. Positive divergence means a source; negative means a sink. The divergence theorem converts a volume integral of $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A}$ into the flux of $\mathbf{A}$ through the closed surface — the differential form of Gauss’s law follows from it.

topics.title: Electric Potential & Energy Density
topics.preamble:
**(J) Potential — basic definitions**

$$
V_{AB}=V_{A}-V_{B}=-\int_{B}^{A}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L},\qquad
W=Q(V_{B}-V_{A})
$$

**(K) Potential of standard configurations**

| Source | Potential | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Point charge $Q$ | $V=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R}$ | $V=0$ at $R=\infty$ |
| Line charge $\rho_{L}$ | $V_{A}-V_{B}=\dfrac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\ln\dfrac{\rho_{B}}{\rho_{A}}$ | $V=0$ at $\infty$ is impossible; use a finite reference |
| Sheet charge $\rho_{s}$ | $V_{A}-V_{B}=-\dfrac{\rho_{s}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(x_{A}-x_{B})$ | sheet at $x=0$, valid for $x>0$ |

Also $\displaystyle\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=0$ in electrostatics.

**Critical note.** For a line charge, $V\to\infty$ as $\rho\to\infty$ — infinity cannot be the zero reference. Every line-charge potential problem must therefore quote a finite reference point, and the answer is always found as a difference.

**(L) Gradient and the field–potential relations**

$$
\mathbf{E}=-\nabla V,\qquad \rho_{v}=\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}=-\varepsilon\nabla^{2}V
$$

Cartesian:
$$
\nabla V=\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{a}_{x}+\frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{a}_{y}+\frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{a}_{z}
$$

Spherical:
$$
\nabla V=\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}\hat{a}_{r}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial V}{\partial\theta}\hat{a}_{\theta}+\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial V}{\partial\phi}\hat{a}_{\phi}
$$

**(M) Energy and energy density**

$$
W_{E}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{n}Q_{k}V_{k}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{v}\rho_{v}V\,dv=\frac{1}{2}\int_{v}\mathbf{D}\cdot\mathbf{E}\,dv
$$

$$
w_{E}=\frac{dW_{E}}{dv}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{D}\cdot\mathbf{E}=\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon E^{2}=\frac{D^{2}}{2\varepsilon}\ \mathrm{J/m^{3}}
$$

topics.examDefinition: Electric flux density (electric displacement) $\mathbf{D}$ is useful because Gauss’s law is simplest in terms of $\mathbf{D}$. In free space $\mathbf{D}=\varepsilon_{0}\mathbf{E}$; in linear dielectrics $\mathbf{D}=\varepsilon\mathbf{E}$. The SI unit of $\mathbf{D}$ is $\mathrm{C/m}^{2}$.

topics.title: Electric Dipole & Polarization
topics.preamble:
**(N) Dipole results (derived in Question 1 below)**

$$
V=\frac{Qd\cos\theta}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}=\frac{p\cos\theta}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}=\frac{\mathbf{p}\cdot\hat{a}_{r}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}}\qquad(r\gg d)
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}=\frac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{3}}\bigl(2\cos\theta\,\hat{a}_{r}+\sin\theta\,\hat{a}_{\theta}\bigr),\qquad
|\mathbf{E}|=\frac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{3}}\sqrt{1+3\cos^{2}\theta}
$$

Vector (coordinate-free) form — useful when $\mathbf{p}$ is not along $\hat{a}_{z}$:
$$
\mathbf{E}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{3}}\bigl[3(\mathbf{p}\cdot\hat{a}_{r})\hat{a}_{r}-\mathbf{p}\bigr]
$$

Decay rates — worth memorising:
- point charge: $V\propto 1/r$, $E\propto 1/r^{2}$
- dipole: $V\propto 1/r^{2}$, $E\propto 1/r^{3}$

**(O) Polarization and the dielectric relations**

$$
\mathbf{P}=\lim_{\Delta v\to 0}\frac{\sum_{k}\mathbf{p}_{k}}{\Delta v}\qquad\text{(dipole moment per unit volume, }\mathrm{C/m^{2}}\text{)}
$$

$$
\mathbf{P}=\varepsilon_{0}\chi_{e}\mathbf{E},\qquad
\mathbf{D}=\varepsilon_{0}\mathbf{E}+\mathbf{P}=\varepsilon_{0}(1+\chi_{e})\mathbf{E}=\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}\mathbf{E}
$$

$$
\varepsilon_{r}=1+\chi_{e}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbf{P}=\varepsilon_{0}(\varepsilon_{r}-1)\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{D}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{r}}\Bigr)
$$

topics.title: Electric Boundary Conditions
topics.preamble:
**(P) Derivation of the boundary conditions between two dielectrics**

Consider the interface between two perfect dielectrics of permittivities $\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r1}$ (medium 1) and $\varepsilon_{2}=\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r2}$ (medium 2).

**Condition 1 — tangential component of $\mathbf{E}$.** Apply the conservative property $\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=0$ to a small rectangular loop straddling the interface, of width $\Delta w$ along the boundary and height $\Delta h$ perpendicular to it:
$$
\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=E_{t1}\Delta w-E_{t2}\Delta w+(\text{terms }\propto\Delta h)=0
$$
Now shrink the loop onto the boundary, $\Delta h\to 0$. The contributions of the two vertical sides vanish, leaving
$$
E_{t1}\Delta w=E_{t2}\Delta w\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E_{t1}=E_{t2}
$$
and
$$
\frac{D_{t1}}{\varepsilon_{1}}=\frac{D_{t2}}{\varepsilon_{2}}
$$
The tangential component of $\mathbf{E}$ is continuous across the boundary.

**Condition 2 — normal component of $\mathbf{D}$.** Apply Gauss’s law $\oint\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}$ to a small pillbox of face area $\Delta S$ and height $\Delta h$ straddling the interface:
$$
\oint\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=D_{n1}\Delta S-D_{n2}\Delta S+(\text{side walls}\to 0\text{ as }\Delta h\to 0)=\rho_{s}\Delta S
$$
$$
D_{n1}-D_{n2}=\rho_{s}
$$
For two perfect dielectrics there is no free surface charge ($\rho_{s}=0$), so
$$
D_{n1}=D_{n2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\varepsilon_{1}E_{n1}=\varepsilon_{2}E_{n2}
$$
The normal component of $\mathbf{D}$ is continuous across a charge-free boundary.

**(Q) Law of refraction of the electric field**

Let $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ be measured from the normal to the interface. Then
$$
\tan\theta_{1}=\frac{E_{t1}}{E_{n1}},\qquad\tan\theta_{2}=\frac{E_{t2}}{E_{n2}}
$$
Dividing and using $E_{t1}=E_{t2}$ together with $\varepsilon_{1}E_{n1}=\varepsilon_{2}E_{n2}$:
$$
\frac{\tan\theta_{1}}{\tan\theta_{2}}=\frac{E_{n2}}{E_{n1}}=\frac{\varepsilon_{1}}{\varepsilon_{2}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\tan\theta_{1}}{\tan\theta_{2}}=\frac{\varepsilon_{r1}}{\varepsilon_{r2}}
$$

**(R) The working method — used in every problem below**

1. Identify the normal direction from the equation of the boundary plane ($z=0\Rightarrow\hat{a}_{z}$; $y=0\Rightarrow\hat{a}_{y}$; $x=0\Rightarrow\hat{a}_{x}$). The other two directions are tangential.
2. Split the given field into its normal and tangential parts.
3. Carry the tangential $\mathbf{E}$ across unchanged.
4. Carry the normal $\mathbf{D}$ across unchanged.
5. Reassemble, then convert between $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ as required.

Useful shortcut for polarization: $\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{D}-\varepsilon_{0}\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{D}\bigl(1-\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_{r}}\bigr)$ — avoids computing $\mathbf{E}$ first.

topics.title: Current Density, Continuity Equation & Relaxation Time
topics.preamble:
**(S) Current and current density**

$$
I = \int_{S}\mathbf{J}\cdot d\mathbf{S},\qquad
\mathbf{J}=\sigma\mathbf{E}\quad\text{(conduction, point form of Ohm’s law)},\qquad
\mathbf{J}=\rho_{v}\mathbf{u}\quad\text{(convection)}
$$

**(T) Continuity equation**

$$
\oint_{S}\mathbf{J}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=-\frac{dQ_{i}}{dt}\quad\text{(integral form)},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=-\frac{\partial\rho_{v}}{\partial t}\quad\text{(point form)}
$$

**(U) Relaxation time**

$$
\rho_{v}=\rho_{v0}\,e^{-t/\tau},\qquad
\tau=\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma}\ \text{(seconds)}
$$

**Method note.** For a surface integral $\mathbf{J}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ on a constant-coordinate surface, only one component of $\mathbf{J}$ survives — the one parallel to $d\mathbf{S}$. All other components are automatically discarded by the dot product, so do not waste time on them.

topics.title: Poisson’s & Laplace’s Equations, Capacitance & Uniqueness Theorem
topics.preamble:
**(V) Poisson’s and Laplace’s equations**

$$
\nabla^{2}V=-\frac{\rho_{v}}{\varepsilon}\quad\text{(Poisson)},\qquad
\nabla^{2}V=0\quad\text{(Laplace, charge-free region)}
$$

**(W) The Laplacian operator**

Cartesian:

$$
\nabla^{2}V=\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial y^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial z^{2}}
$$

Cylindrical:

$$
\nabla^{2}V=\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\!\left(\rho\frac{\partial V}{\partial\rho}\right)+\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\phi^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial z^{2}}
$$

Spherical:

$$
\nabla^{2}V=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\!\left(r^{2}\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}\right)
+\frac{1}{r^{2}\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\!\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial V}{\partial\theta}\right)
+\frac{1}{r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\phi^{2}}
$$

**(X) The five-step recipe for every capacitance derivation**

1. Choose the coordinate system matching the symmetry; assume $V$ depends on one variable only.
2. Write $\nabla^{2}V=0$ and integrate twice to get $V$ with two constants.
3. Apply the two boundary conditions to fix the constants.
4. Find $\mathbf{E}=-\nabla V$, then $\mathbf{D}=\varepsilon\mathbf{E}$, then $\rho_{s}=D_{N}$ at a conductor surface, then $Q=\int_{S}\rho_{s}\,dS$.
5. Form $C=Q/V_{0}$ — the potential $V_{0}$ must cancel out.

**(Y) The three standard results (derived below)**

| Capacitor | Geometry | Capacitance |
|---|---|---|
| Parallel plate | area $S$, separation $d$ | $C=\varepsilon S/d$ |
| Coaxial cable | radii $a<b$, length $L$ | $C=2\pi\varepsilon L/\ln(b/a)$ |
| Spherical | radii $a<b$ | $C=4\pi\varepsilon/\bigl(1/a-1/b\bigr)=4\pi\varepsilon ab/(b-a)$ |

topics.title: Reference Formulas for Chapter 3
topics.preamble: **(A) Biot–Savart law** $$ \mathrm{d}\mathbf{H}=\frac{I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}\times\hat{a}_{R}}{4\pi R^{2}}=\frac{I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}\times\mathbf{R}}{4\pi R^{3}}\quad(\mathrm{A/m}) $$ where $\mathbf{R}$ runs from the current element to the field point. **(B) Straight filament of finite length — the workhorse formula** $$ \mathbf{H}=\frac{I}{4\pi\rho}\bigl(\sin\alpha_{2}-\sin\alpha_{1}\bigr)\,\hat{a}_{\phi} $$ - $\rho$ = perpendicular distance from the filament to the field point; - drop a perpendicular from the field point onto the filament — its foot is the origin for measuring $\alpha$; - $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ are the angles subtended at the field point by the start and end of the filament, measured from that perpendicular, and taken positive in the direction of current flow; - $\hat{a}_{\phi}=\hat{a}_{L}\times\hat{a}_{\rho}$, where $\hat{a}_{L}$ is the unit vector along the current direction and $\hat{a}_{\rho}$ points from the foot toward the field point. Infinite filament: $\alpha_{1}=-90^{\circ}$, $\alpha_{2}=+90^{\circ}$, giving $$ \mathbf{H}=\frac{I}{2\pi\rho}\,\hat{a}_{\phi} $$ Semi-infinite filament (one end at the perpendicular foot, the other at infinity): $\mathbf{H}=\dfrac{I}{4\pi\rho}\,\hat{a}_{\phi}$ — exactly half. **(C) Ampere’s circuital law** $$ \oint_{L}\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}=I_{\mathrm{enc}}\qquad\text{(integral form)},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}\qquad\text{(point form)} $$ **(D) Curl operator** Cartesian: $$ \nabla\times\mathbf{H} =\left(\frac{\partial H_{z}}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial H_{y}}{\partial z}\right)\hat{a}_{x} +\left(\frac{\partial H_{x}}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial H_{z}}{\partial x}\right)\hat{a}_{y} +\left(\frac{\partial H_{y}}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial H_{x}}{\partial y}\right)\hat{a}_{z} $$ Cylindrical: $$ \nabla\times\mathbf{H} =\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial H_{z}}{\partial\phi}-\frac{\partial H_{\phi}}{\partial z}\right)\hat{a}_{\rho} +\left(\frac{\partial H_{\rho}}{\partial z}-\frac{\partial H_{z}}{\partial\rho}\right)\hat{a}_{\phi} +\frac{1}{\rho}\left(\frac{\partial(\rho H_{\phi})}{\partial\rho}-\frac{\partial H_{\rho}}{\partial\phi}\right)\hat{a}_{z} $$ **(E) Magnetic force** $$ \mathbf{F}=I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}\times\mathbf{B},\qquad \mathbf{B}=\mu\mathbf{H},\qquad \mu_{0}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{H/m} $$ Useful: $\mu_{0}/(2\pi)=2\times10^{-7}$. **(F) Cross-product table — get these right or lose the marks** Cyclic (positive): $$ \hat{a}_{x}\times\hat{a}_{y}=\hat{a}_{z},\qquad \hat{a}_{y}\times\hat{a}_{z}=\hat{a}_{x},\qquad \hat{a}_{z}\times\hat{a}_{x}=\hat{a}_{y} $$ Anti-cyclic (negative): $$ \hat{a}_{y}\times\hat{a}_{x}=-\hat{a}_{z},\qquad \hat{a}_{z}\times\hat{a}_{y}=-\hat{a}_{x},\qquad \hat{a}_{x}\times\hat{a}_{z}=-\hat{a}_{y} $$ **(G) Converting $\hat{a}_{\phi}$ to Cartesian** $$ \hat{a}_{\phi}=-\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{x}+\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{y}, \qquad \cos\phi=\frac{x}{\rho},\quad\sin\phi=\frac{y}{\rho} $$

topics.title: Curl & Stokes’s Theorem
topics.preamble:
**(H) Definition of curl**

$$
(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})\cdot\hat{a}_{N}
=\lim_{\Delta S_{N}\to 0}\frac{\oint_{L}\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}}{\Delta S_{N}}
$$

The curl is a vector whose component in any direction $\hat{a}_{N}$ is the circulation of the field per unit area, in the limit of vanishing area oriented normal to $\hat{a}_{N}$.

**(I) Stokes’s theorem**

$$
\oint_{L}\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}=\int_{S}(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
$$

$S$ is any surface bounded by the closed path $L$; the sense of $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}$ and the direction of traversal of $L$ must obey the right-hand rule.

**(J) Curl in spherical coordinates**

$$
(\nabla\times\mathbf{A})_{r}=\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\left(\frac{\partial(A_{\phi}\sin\theta)}{\partial\theta}-\frac{\partial A_{\theta}}{\partial\phi}\right)
$$

$$
(\nabla\times\mathbf{A})_{\theta}=\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial A_{r}}{\partial\phi}-\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(r A_{\phi})}{\partial r}
$$

$$
(\nabla\times\mathbf{A})_{\phi}=\frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\partial(r A_{\theta})}{\partial r}-\frac{\partial A_{r}}{\partial\theta}\right)
$$

**(K) Differential surface elements — needed for the right-hand side**

| Surface | $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}$ | Boundary element $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Plane $z=\mathrm{const}$ | $\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\,\hat{a}_{z}$ | $\mathrm{d}x\hat{a}_{x}$ or $\mathrm{d}y\hat{a}_{y}$ |
| Cylinder $\rho=\mathrm{const}$ | $\rho\,\mathrm{d}\phi\,\mathrm{d}z\,\hat{a}_{\rho}$ | $\rho\,\mathrm{d}\phi\hat{a}_{\phi}$ or $\mathrm{d}z\hat{a}_{z}$ |
| Sphere $r=\mathrm{const}$ | $r^{2}\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\,\mathrm{d}\phi\,\hat{a}_{r}$ | $r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\hat{a}_{\theta}$ or $r\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\phi\hat{a}_{\phi}$ |
| Cone $\theta=\mathrm{const}$ | $r\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\phi\,\hat{a}_{\theta}$ | $\mathrm{d}r\hat{a}_{r}$ or $r\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}\phi\hat{a}_{\phi}$ |

topics.title: Scalar & Vector Magnetic Potential
topics.preamble:
**(L) Scalar magnetic potential $V_{m}$**

$$
\mathbf{H}=-\nabla V_{m}\qquad\text{(valid ONLY where }\mathbf{J}=\mathbf{0}\text{)}
$$

Why the restriction? Because $\nabla\times(\nabla V_{m})\equiv\mathbf{0}$ identically, while $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}$. Compatible only if $\mathbf{J}=\mathbf{0}$. In a current-free region $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ then gives Laplace’s equation:

$$
\nabla^{2}V_{m}=0\qquad\text{(units of }V_{m}\text{: amperes)}
$$

**(M) Vector magnetic potential $\mathbf{A}$**

$$
\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}\qquad\text{(valid EVERYWHERE)}
$$

Why no restriction? Because $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{A})\equiv 0$ identically, and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ always holds.

$$
\mathbf{A}=\frac{\mu I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}}{4\pi R}\quad\text{(filament)},\qquad
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{A}=-\mu\mathbf{J},\qquad
\Phi=\int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}=\oint_{L}\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}
$$

(units of $\mathbf{A}$: Wb/m)

**(N) Magnetic boundary conditions**

$$
B_{N1}=B_{N2}\implies\mu_{1}H_{N1}=\mu_{2}H_{N2}
$$

$$

topics.preamble: **(A) Faraday’s law** $$ \mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\quad\text{(volts)},\qquad \mathcal{E} = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\quad\text{($N$ turns)},\qquad \oint_{L}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L} = -\frac{d}{dt}\int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S} $$ with flux $$ \Phi = \int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}. $$ **(B) The three ways flux can change** | Case | Name | EMF | |------|------|-----| | Loop fixed, $\mathbf{B}$ varies | transformer emf | $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}=-\int_{S}\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ | | Loop moves, $\mathbf{B}$ static | motional emf | $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}=\oint_{L}(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot d\mathbf{L}$ | | Both | general case | $\displaystyle\mathcal{E}=-\int_{S}\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}\cdot d\mathbf{S}+\oint_{L}(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot d\mathbf{L}$ | For a straight bar of length $L$ moving with speed $v$ perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$: $\mathcal{E}=BLv$. **(C) Maxwell’s equations — time-varying fields** | Law | Point form | Integral form | |-----|------------|---------------| | Faraday | $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\dfrac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}$ | $\displaystyle\oint_{L}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=-\dfrac{d}{dt}\int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ | | Ampere (corrected) | $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\dfrac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}$ | $\displaystyle\oint_{L}\mathbf{H}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=\int_{S}\left(\mathbf{J}+\dfrac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\right)\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ | | Gauss (electric) | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}=\rho_{v}$ | $\displaystyle\oint_{S}\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}$ | | Gauss (magnetic) | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ | $\displaystyle\oint_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=0$ | **(D) Phasor form** (time-harmonic, $e^{j\omega t}$: replace $\partial/\partial t\to j\omega$) $$ \nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu\mathbf{H}_{s},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=\frac{\rho_{vs}}{\varepsilon},\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{H}_{s}=0. $$ **(E) The two current densities** $$ \mathbf{J}_{c}=\sigma\mathbf{E}\quad\text{(conduction)},\qquad \mathbf{J}_{d}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}=\varepsilon\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}\quad\text{(displacement)}. $$ **(F) Loss tangent** (for $E=E_{0}\cos\omega t$) $$ \frac{|\mathbf{J}_{c}|}{|\mathbf{J}_{d}|}=\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}=\frac{\sigma}{2\pi f\varepsilon}=\tan\delta. $$ Crossover: $f=\sigma/(2\pi\varepsilon)$. topics.examDefinition: Maxwell’s equations unify electrostatics, magnetostatics, and induction, including displacement current. They exist in integral form (global) and point (differential) form. In free space with no charges/currents they support plane electromagnetic waves with $E/H=\eta_{0}$.

topics.title: Reference Formulas for Chapter 5
topics.preamble: **(A) The wave equation and Helmholtz’s equation** $$ \nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}=\mu\varepsilon\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^{2}}\quad\text{(lossless, time domain)} $$ $$ \nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}=\gamma^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad \nabla^{2}\mathbf{H}_{s}=\gamma^{2}\mathbf{H}_{s}\quad\text{(Helmholtz, phasor form)} $$ **(B) Propagation constant** $$ \gamma=\alpha+j\beta=\sqrt{j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)} $$ $$ \alpha=\omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\varepsilon}{2}\left(\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^{2}}-1\right)}\quad\text{(Np/m)} $$ $$ \beta=\omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\varepsilon}{2}\left(\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^{2}}+1\right)}\quad\text{(rad/m)} $$ **(C) Intrinsic impedance** $$ \eta=\sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon}}=|\eta|\angle\theta_{\eta}\ \Omega $$ **(D) Wave parameters** $$ u=\frac{\omega}{\beta}\ \text{(m/s)},\qquad \lambda=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}=\frac{u}{f}\ \text{(m)},\qquad \delta=\frac{1}{\alpha}\ \text{(skin depth, m)} $$ **(E) The three standard media** — specialise, never re-derive | Quantity | Free space ($\sigma=0$) | Lossless dielectric ($\sigma=0$) | Good conductor ($\sigma\gg\omega\varepsilon$) | |----------|-------------------------|-----------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | $\alpha$ | $0$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}$ | | $\beta$ | $\omega\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}$ | $\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$ | $\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}$ | | $\eta$ | $377\,\Omega$ | $\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$ | $\sqrt{\omega\mu/\sigma}\,\angle 45^{\circ}$ | | $u$ | $3\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ | $1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$ | $2\omega/\mu\sigma$ (equiv. $\omega\delta$) | Note that in a good conductor $\alpha=\beta$, and $\mathbf{H}$ lags $\mathbf{E}$ by exactly $45^{\circ}$. **(F) Loss tangent** — decides which column applies $$ \tan\delta=\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon} \begin{cases} \ll 1 & \text{good dielectric}\\ \gg 1 & \text{good conductor} \end{cases} $$ **(G) Constants** $$ \eta_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\varepsilon_{0}}}=120\pi\approx 377\,\Omega,\qquad c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}}=3\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s} $$ **(H) Key vector identity** (used in every derivation below) $$ \nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{A}=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A})-\nabla^{2}\mathbf{A} $$ **(I) Poynting vector** $$ \mathbf{P}=\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}\ \mathrm{W/m}^{2}\quad\text{(instantaneous)} $$ $$ \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Re}\{\mathbf{E}_{s}\times\mathbf{H}_{s}^{*}\}\quad\text{(time-average, phasor)} $$ **(J) Poynting’s theorem** $$ \oint_{S}(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H})\cdot d\mathbf{S} =-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{v}\left(\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon E^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mu H^{2}\right)\,dv -\int_{v}\sigma E^{2}\,dv $$ **(K) Time-average power density of a plane wave** $$ \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2|\eta|}e^{-2\alpha z}\cos\theta_{\eta}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z} \quad\text{(lossy)} $$ $$ \mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2\eta}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z} \quad\text{(lossless: $\alpha=0$, $\theta_{\eta}=0$)} $$ **(L) Skin depth and good-conductor formulas** $$ \delta=\frac{1}{\alpha}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}},\qquad \alpha=\beta=\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma},\qquad \gamma=(1+j)\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma} $$ $$ \eta=\sqrt{\frac{\omega\mu}{\sigma}}\,\angle 45^{\circ},\qquad u=\frac{\omega}{\beta}=\omega\delta,\qquad \lambda=2\pi\delta $$ **(M) Good-dielectric approximations** ($\tan\delta\ll 1$) $$ \alpha\approx\frac{\sigma}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}},\qquad \beta\approx\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon},\qquad \eta\approx\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}} $$ **(N) Standard method for numerical UPW problems** 1. Read the phase to get $\beta$ and direction: $\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\Rightarrow +\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$; $\cos(\omega t+\beta z)\Rightarrow -\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$. 2. Medium: $u=c/\sqrt{\mu_{r}\varepsilon_{r}}$, $\beta=\omega/u$, $\lambda=2\pi/\beta=u/f$, $\eta=\eta_{0}\sqrt{\mu_{r}/\varepsilon_{r}}$. 3. Cross-multiply: $\mathbf{H}=(1/\eta)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}\times\mathbf{E}$, or $\mathbf{E}=\eta\,\mathbf{H}\times\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}$. 4. Check $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}\parallel\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}$ and $|\mathbf{E}|/|\mathbf{H}|=\eta$. 5. Phasors: $\cos(\omega t-\beta z+\phi)\leftrightarrow E_{0}\angle\phi\,e^{-j\beta z}$. **(O) Normal incidence** (region 1 $\to$ region 2) $$ \Gamma=\frac{E_{r0}}{E_{i0}}=\frac{\eta_{2}-\eta_{1}}{\eta_{2}+\eta_{1}},\qquad \tau=\frac{E_{t0}}{E_{i0}}=\frac{2\eta_{2}}{\eta_{2}+\eta_{1}},\qquad 1+\Gamma=\tau $$ | Case | $\Gamma$ | $\tau$ | Meaning | |------|----------|--------|---------| | $\eta_{2}=\eta_{1}$ (matched) | $0$ | $1$ | no reflection | | $\eta_{2}=0$ (PEC) | $-1$ | $0$ | total reflection, phase reversed | | $\eta_{2}=\infty$ | $+1$ | $2$ | total reflection, no reversal | **(P) Standing wave ratio** $$ s=\frac{|E|_{\max}}{|E|_{\min}}=\frac{1+|\Gamma|}{1-|\Gamma|},\qquad |\Gamma|=\frac{s-1}{s+1},\qquad 1\le s\le\infty $$ Spacing: adjacent maxima (or minima) are $\lambda/2$ apart; max to adjacent min is $\lambda/4$. **(Q) Input (wave) impedance of a slab of thickness $d$** $$ \eta_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta_{2}\frac{\eta_{3}\cos\beta_{2}d+j\eta_{2}\sin\beta_{2}d}{\eta_{2}\cos\beta_{2}d+j\eta_{3}\sin\beta_{2}d} $$ $$ d=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{4}:\ \eta_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{\eta_{2}^{2}}{\eta_{3}} \quad\text{(quarter-wave)};\qquad d=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{2}:\ \eta_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta_{3} \quad\text{(half-wave window)} $$ ---

topics.examDefinition: At normal incidence on a dielectric interface, part of the wave reflects and part transmits. Reflection and transmission coefficients follow from continuity of tangential $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$. For $\eta_{2}<\eta_{1}$ (e.g. denser dielectric), $\Gamma$ is negative (phase reversal of $E_{r}$).

topics.title: Reference Formulas for Chapter 6
topics.preamble: **(A) Primary constants** — per unit length of line $$ R\ (\Omega/\mathrm{m}),\quad L\ (\mathrm{H/m}),\quad G\ (\mathrm{S/m}),\quad C\ (\mathrm{F/m}) $$ **(B) Secondary constants** — derived from the primary ones $$ \gamma=\alpha+j\beta=\sqrt{(R+j\omega L)(G+j\omega C)} $$ $$ Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{R+j\omega L}{G+j\omega C}} $$ $$ u=\frac{\omega}{\beta},\qquad \lambda=\frac{2\pi}{\beta} $$ **(C) Inverse relations** — for finding $R,L,G,C$ from $\gamma$ and $Z_{0}$ $$ \gamma Z_{0}=R+j\omega L,\qquad \frac{\gamma}{Z_{0}}=G+j\omega C $$ (multiply to kill the division; divide to kill the multiplication). **(D) The two special lines** | | Lossless ($R=G=0$) | Distortionless ($R/L=G/C$) | |---|---|---| | $\alpha$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{RG}$ (independent of $\omega$) | | $\beta$ | $\omega\sqrt{LC}$ | $\omega\sqrt{LC}$ | | $\gamma$ | $j\omega\sqrt{LC}$ | $\sqrt{RG}+j\omega\sqrt{LC}$ | | $Z_{0}$ | $\sqrt{L/C}$ (real) | $\sqrt{L/C}$ (real) | | $u$ | $1/\sqrt{LC}$ | $1/\sqrt{LC}$ | **(E) Input impedance** of a line of length $\ell$ terminated in $Z_{L}$ $$ Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{L}+jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell}{Z_{0}+jZ_{L}\tan\beta\ell}\qquad\text{(lossless)} $$ $$ Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{L}+Z_{0}\tanh\gamma\ell}{Z_{0}+Z_{L}\tanh\gamma\ell}\qquad\text{(lossy)} $$ **(F) Reflection coefficient and SWR** $$ \Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}},\qquad s=\frac{1+|\Gamma_{L}|}{1-|\Gamma_{L}|} $$ **(G) Special cases worth knowing by sight** | Condition | $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ | Name | |---|---|---| | $\ell=\lambda/2$ (or any $n\lambda/2$) | $Z_{L}$ | half-wave repeater | | $\ell=\lambda/4$ | $Z_{0}^{2}/Z_{L}$ | quarter-wave transformer | | $Z_{L}=Z_{0}$ | $Z_{0}$ | matched — no reflection | | $Z_{L}=0$ (short) | $jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell$ | purely reactive | | $Z_{L}=\infty$ (open) | $-jZ_{0}\cot\beta\ell$ | purely reactive | Note the exact parallel with Chapter 5: $Z_{0}\leftrightarrow\eta$, $Z_{L}\leftrightarrow\eta_{3}$, $Z_{\mathrm{in}}\leftrightarrow\eta_{\mathrm{in}}$. The transmission-line formulas are the plane-wave formulas wearing different symbols.

topics.examDefinition: Lossless lines have $R=G=0$ (no attenuation). Lossy lines have $\alpha>0$. A distortionless line satisfies $R/L=G/C$, so $\alpha$ is frequency-independent and $v_{p}$ is constant — pulses keep their shape. Telephone lines historically targeted this condition.

topics.title: Input Impedance, Reflection Coefficient & SWR
topics.preamble:
**(H) Voltage along a lossless line** (with $d$ measured from the load)

$$
V(d)=V_{0}^{+}\!\left(e^{j\beta d}+\Gamma_{L}e^{-j\beta d}\right)
$$

$$
V_{L}=V_{0}^{+}(1+\Gamma_{L})\qquad\text{(at }d=0\text{)}
$$

$$
|V|_{\max}=|V_{0}^{+}|(1+|\Gamma_{L}|),\qquad |V|_{\min}=|V_{0}^{+}|(1-|\Gamma_{L}|),\qquad s=\frac{|V|_{\max}}{|V|_{\min}}
$$

First voltage maximum from the load (where $\Gamma_{L}=|\Gamma_{L}|\angle\phi$):

$$
d_{\max}=\frac{\phi}{2\beta}=\frac{\phi_{\mathrm{rad}}\,\lambda}{4\pi}
$$

**(I) Source end — the line reduces to $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$**

$$
V_{\mathrm{in}}=V_{g}\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}}{Z_{g}+Z_{\mathrm{in}}},\qquad I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{V_{g}}{Z_{g}+Z_{\mathrm{in}}}
$$

**(J) Power**

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Re}\{VI^{*}\}=\frac{1}{2}|V|^{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left\{\frac{1}{Z^{*}}\right\}=\frac{1}{2}|I|^{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\{Z\}
$$

$$
P_{L}=\frac{|V_{L}|^{2}}{2R_{L}}\qquad\text{(resistive load)}
$$

On a lossless line all power entering the input reaches the load: $P_{\mathrm{in}}=P_{L}$ — a free check on every such problem.

questions.text: Find the vector that extends from $A(-3,-4,6)$ to $B(-5,2,-8)$ and express it in the cylindrical coordinate system.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Find the distance vector in Cartesian form**

The vector extending from point $A$ to point $B$ is the difference of the position vectors, $\mathbf{R}_{AB} = \mathbf{r}_{B}-\mathbf{r}_{A}$:

$$
\mathbf{R}_{AB} = (x_{B}-x_{A})\hat{a}_{x} + (y_{B}-y_{A})\hat{a}_{y} + (z_{B}-z_{A})\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
= \bigl[-5-(-3)\bigr]\hat{a}_{x} + \bigl[2-(-4)\bigr]\hat{a}_{y} + \bigl[-8-6\bigr]\hat{a}_{z}
= -2\hat{a}_{x} + 6\hat{a}_{y} - 14\hat{a}_{z}
$$

So $A_{x}=-2$, $A_{y}=6$, $A_{z}=-14$.

**Step 2 — Locate the point at which the transformation is performed**

A cylindrical unit vector $(\hat{a}_{\rho},\hat{a}_{\phi})$ has a direction that depends on position, so we must state where the vector is being expressed. The vector originates at $A$, hence we transform at $A(-3,-4,6)$:

$$
\rho_{A} = \sqrt{x_{A}^{2}+y_{A}^{2}} = \sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-4)^{2}} = \sqrt{9+16} = \sqrt{25} = 5
$$

Since $x_{A}=-3<0$ and $y_{A}=-4<0$, point $A$ lies in the third quadrant:

$$
\phi_{A} = 180^{\circ} + \tan^{-1}\!\frac{|-4|}{|-3|} = 180^{\circ}+53.13^{\circ} = 233.13^{\circ}
$$

Rather than using the angle, we use the exact ratios (safer):

$$
\cos\phi_{A} = \frac{x_{A}}{\rho_{A}} = \frac{-3}{5} = -0.6,\qquad
\sin\phi_{A} = \frac{y_{A}}{\rho_{A}} = \frac{-4}{5} = -0.8
$$

**Step 3 — Transform the components using formula (B)**

$$
A_{\rho} = A_{x}\cos\phi + A_{y}\sin\phi = (-2)(-0.6)+(6)(-0.8) = 1.2-4.8 = -3.6
$$

$$
A_{\phi} = -A_{x}\sin\phi + A_{y}\cos\phi = -(-2)(-0.8)+(6)(-0.6) = -1.6-3.6 = -5.2
$$

$$
A_{z} = -14
$$

(unchanged — $\hat{a}_{z}$ is common to both systems)

**Step 4 — Verification by magnitude**

A coordinate transformation is a rotation, so the magnitude must be preserved:

$$
|\mathbf{R}|_{\mathrm{cart}} = \sqrt{(-2)^{2}+6^{2}+(-14)^{2}} = \sqrt{4+36+196} = \sqrt{236} = 15.362
$$

$$
|\mathbf{R}|_{\mathrm{cyl}} = \sqrt{(-3.6)^{2}+(-5.2)^{2}+(-14)^{2}} = \sqrt{12.96+27.04+196} = \sqrt{236} = 15.362
$$

The magnitudes agree, confirming the transformation.

questions.text: Transform the vector $\mathbf{A} = 4\hat{a}_{x}-2\hat{a}_{y}-4\hat{a}_{z}$ into spherical coordinates at the point $P(x=-2,\ y=-3,\ z=4)$.
Transform the vector field $\mathbf{A} = 4\hat{a}_{x}-2\hat{a}_{y}-4\hat{a}_{z}$ into the cylindrical coordinate system at the point $P(2,3,5)$.
Given the point $P(-3,4,5)$, express the vector that extends from $P$ to $Q(2,0,-1)$ in (a) rectangular, (b) cylindrical, and (c) spherical coordinates.
Transform $\mathbf{H} = 20\hat{a}_{\rho}-10\hat{a}_{\phi}+3\hat{a}_{z}$ A/m into the Cartesian coordinate system at $P(x=5,\ y=2,\ z=-1)$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Identify the direction of transformation**

Here the field is given in cylindrical form and must be converted to Cartesian, so formula (C) applies:

$$
H_{x} = H_{\rho}\cos\phi - H_{\phi}\sin\phi,\qquad
H_{y} = H_{\rho}\sin\phi + H_{\phi}\cos\phi,\qquad
H_{z} = H_{z}
$$

**Step 2 — Find $\cos\phi$ and $\sin\phi$ at $P$**

The point is given in Cartesian form, so:

$$
\rho = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} = \sqrt{5^{2}+2^{2}} = \sqrt{25+4} = \sqrt{29} = 5.385
$$

$x=5>0$, $y=2>0$ ⇒ first quadrant:

$$
\phi = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{2}{5} = 21.80^{\circ}
$$

$$
\cos\phi = \frac{x}{\rho} = \frac{5}{5.385} = 0.9285,\qquad
\sin\phi = \frac{y}{\rho} = \frac{2}{5.385} = 0.3714
$$

**Step 3 — Substitute $H_{\rho}=20$, $H_{\phi}=-10$, $H_{z}=3$**

$$
H_{x} = (20)(0.9285)-(-10)(0.3714) = 18.570+3.714 = 22.284\ \mathrm{A/m}
$$

$$
H_{y} = (20)(0.3714)+(-10)(0.9285) = 7.428-9.285 = -1.857\ \mathrm{A/m}
$$

$$
H_{z} = 3\ \mathrm{A/m}
$$

**Step 4 — Verification**

$$
|\mathbf{H}|_{\mathrm{cyl}} = \sqrt{20^{2}+(-10)^{2}+3^{2}} = \sqrt{400+100+9} = \sqrt{509} = 22.561
$$

$$
|\mathbf{H}|_{\mathrm{cart}} = \sqrt{(22.284)^{2}+(-1.857)^{2}+3^{2}} = \sqrt{496.58+3.45+9} = \sqrt{509.03} = 22.561\ \checkmark
$$

questions.text: Transform $\mathbf{F} = 10\hat{a}_{x}-8\hat{a}_{y}+6\hat{a}_{z}$ at the point $P(x=10,\ y=-8,\ z=6)$ into the cylindrical coordinate system.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Cylindrical coordinates of $P$**

$$
\rho = \sqrt{10^{2}+(-8)^{2}} = \sqrt{100+64} = \sqrt{164} = 12.806
$$

$x=10>0$, $y=-8<0$ ⇒ fourth quadrant:

$$
\phi = 360^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\!\frac{8}{10} = 360^{\circ}-38.66^{\circ} = 321.34^{\circ}
\quad\text{(equivalently }-38.66^{\circ}\text{)}
$$

$$
\cos\phi = \frac{10}{12.806} = 0.7809,\qquad
\sin\phi = \frac{-8}{12.806} = -0.6247
$$

**Step 2 — Transform using (B) with $F_{x}=10$, $F_{y}=-8$, $F_{z}=6$**

$$
F_{\rho} = (10)(0.7809)+(-8)(-0.6247) = 7.809+4.998 = 12.807
$$

$$
F_{\phi} = -(10)(-0.6247)+(-8)(0.7809) = 6.247-6.247 = 0
$$

$$
F_{z} = 6
$$

**Step 3 — Physical interpretation of $F_{\phi}=0$**

This result is not a coincidence. The transverse part of the field, $10\hat{a}_{x}-8\hat{a}_{y}$, is exactly parallel to the transverse part of the position vector of $P$, which is also $10\hat{a}_{x}-8\hat{a}_{y}$. A vector parallel to the radial direction has no $\phi$-component, so $F_{\phi}=0$ and

$$
F_{\rho} = \sqrt{10^{2}+(-8)^{2}} = 12.806,
$$

as obtained.

**Step 4 — Verification**

$$
\sqrt{(12.807)^{2}+0^{2}+6^{2}} = \sqrt{164.02+36} = \sqrt{200} = 14.14 = \sqrt{100+64+36} = \sqrt{200}\ \checkmark
$$

questions.text: Transform $\mathbf{A} = y\hat{a}_{x}-(x+y)\hat{a}_{y}+z\hat{a}_{z}$ at the point $P(-3,4,5)$ into the cylindrical coordinate system.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Evaluate the field components at $P$**

This is a field, so the components must first be evaluated at $P(-3,4,5)$, i.e. $x=-3$, $y=4$, $z=5$:

$$
A_{x} = y = 4,\qquad
A_{y} = -(x+y) = -(-3+4) = -1,\qquad
A_{z} = z = 5
$$

Hence at $P$, $\mathbf{A}=4\hat{a}_{x}-1\hat{a}_{y}+5\hat{a}_{z}$.

**Step 2 — Cylindrical coordinates of $P$**

$$
\rho = \sqrt{(-3)^{2}+4^{2}} = \sqrt{25} = 5
$$

$x=-3<0$, $y=4>0$ ⇒ second quadrant:

$$
\phi = 180^{\circ}-53.13^{\circ} = 126.87^{\circ},\qquad
\cos\phi = \frac{-3}{5} = -0.6,\qquad
\sin\phi = \frac{4}{5} = 0.8
$$

**Step 3 — Transform using (B)**

$$
A_{\rho} = (4)(-0.6)+(-1)(0.8) = -2.4-0.8 = -3.2
$$

$$
A_{\phi} = -(4)(0.8)+(-1)(-0.6) = -3.2+0.6 = -2.6
$$

$$
A_{z} = 5
$$

**Step 4 — Verification**

$$
\sqrt{(-3.2)^{2}+(-2.6)^{2}+5^{2}} = \sqrt{10.24+6.76+25} = \sqrt{42} = 6.481 = \sqrt{4^{2}+(-1)^{2}+5^{2}} = \sqrt{42}\ \checkmark
$$

questions.text: Transform the vector $\mathbf{A} = y\hat{a}_{x}+x\hat{a}_{y}+z\hat{a}_{z}$ into cylindrical coordinates at the point $p(2,45^{\circ},5)$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Note that the point is already given in cylindrical form**

Here $\rho=2$, $\phi=45^{\circ}$, $z=5$. The corresponding Cartesian coordinates are:

$$
x = \rho\cos\phi = 2\cos 45^{\circ} = 2(0.7071) = 1.4142,\qquad
y = \rho\sin\phi = 2\sin 45^{\circ} = 1.4142,\qquad
z = 5
$$

**Step 2 — Derive the general transformation first**

Substituting $A_{x}=y=\rho\sin\phi$ and $A_{y}=x=\rho\cos\phi$ into (B):

$$
A_{\rho} = A_{x}\cos\phi + A_{y}\sin\phi = \rho\sin\phi\cos\phi + \rho\cos\phi\sin\phi = 2\rho\sin\phi\cos\phi = \rho\sin 2\phi
$$

$$
A_{\phi} = -A_{x}\sin\phi + A_{y}\cos\phi = -\rho\sin^{2}\phi + \rho\cos^{2}\phi = \rho(\cos^{2}\phi-\sin^{2}\phi) = \rho\cos 2\phi
$$

$$
A_{z} = z
$$

Therefore, in general:

$$
\mathbf{A} = \rho\sin 2\phi\,\hat{a}_{\rho} + \rho\cos 2\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi} + z\,\hat{a}_{z}
$$

**Step 3 — Evaluate at $p(2,45^{\circ},5)$**

$$
A_{\rho} = \rho\sin 2\phi = 2\sin(90^{\circ}) = 2(1) = 2
$$

$$
A_{\phi} = \rho\cos 2\phi = 2\cos(90^{\circ}) = 2(0) = 0
$$

$$
A_{z} = 5
$$

**Step 4 — Verification**

At $p$, the Cartesian components are $A_{x}=y=1.4142$, $A_{y}=x=1.4142$, $A_{z}=5$:

$$
\sqrt{(1.4142)^{2}+(1.4142)^{2}+5^{2}} = \sqrt{2+2+25} = \sqrt{29} = 5.385
$$

$$
\sqrt{2^{2}+0^{2}+5^{2}} = \sqrt{4+25} = \sqrt{29} = 5.385\ \checkmark
$$

questions.text: Express the scalar potential field $V = x^{2}+2y^{2}+3z^{2}$ in spherical coordinates and find the value of $V$ at the point $(2,60^{\circ},90^{\circ})$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Substitute the spherical-to-Cartesian relations**

$V$ is a scalar, so only the coordinate variables are replaced — no unit-vector transformation is required. Using $x=r\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=r\sin\theta\sin\phi$, $z=r\cos\theta$:

$$
\begin{align*}
V &= x^{2}+2y^{2}+3z^{2} \\
&= (r\sin\theta\cos\phi)^{2} + 2(r\sin\theta\sin\phi)^{2} + 3(r\cos\theta)^{2} \\
&= r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\phi + 2r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta\sin^{2}\phi + 3r^{2}\cos^{2}\theta
\end{align*}
$$

**Step 2 — Simplify**

$$
V = r^{2}\bigl[\sin^{2}\theta(\cos^{2}\phi+2\sin^{2}\phi)+3\cos^{2}\theta\bigr]
$$

Using the identity $\cos^{2}\phi+\sin^{2}\phi=1$, we write

$$
\cos^{2}\phi+2\sin^{2}\phi = (\cos^{2}\phi+\sin^{2}\phi)+\sin^{2}\phi = 1+\sin^{2}\phi.
$$

Hence:

$$
V = r^{2}\bigl[\sin^{2}\theta(1+\sin^{2}\phi)+3\cos^{2}\theta\bigr]
$$

**Step 3 — Evaluate at $(r=2,\ \theta=60^{\circ},\ \phi=90^{\circ})$**

$$
\sin 60^{\circ} = 0.8660 \Rightarrow \sin^{2}60^{\circ} = 0.75,\qquad
\cos 60^{\circ} = 0.5 \Rightarrow \cos^{2}60^{\circ} = 0.25,\qquad
\sin^{2}90^{\circ} = 1
$$

$$
V = (2)^{2}\bigl[0.75(1+1)+3(0.25)\bigr] = 4\bigl[0.75(2)+0.75\bigr] = 4(1.5+0.75) = 4(2.25) = 9\ \mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 4 — Cross-check in Cartesian coordinates**

$$
x = 2\sin 60^{\circ}\cos 90^{\circ} = 0,\qquad
y = 2\sin 60^{\circ}\sin 90^{\circ} = 1.732,\qquad
z = 2\cos 60^{\circ} = 1
$$

$$
V = 0^{2}+2(1.732)^{2}+3(1)^{2} = 0+6+3 = 9\ \mathrm{V}\ \checkmark
$$

questions.text: Given the point $P(-2,6,3)$ and the vector field $\mathbf{A} = y\hat{a}_{x}+(xy+z)\hat{a}_{y}$, express $P$ and $\mathbf{A}$ in the spherical coordinate system.

Given points $A(\rho=5,\ \phi=70^{\circ},\ z=-3)$ and $B(\rho=2,\ \phi=-30^{\circ},\ z=1)$, find: (a) a unit vector in Cartesian coordinates at $A$ directed toward $B$; and (b) a unit vector in cylindrical coordinates at $A$ directed toward $B$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Convert both points to Cartesian coordinates**

For $A$:

$$
x_{A} = \rho_{A}\cos\phi_{A} = 5\cos 70^{\circ} = 5(0.3420) = 1.710
$$

$$
y_{A} = \rho_{A}\sin\phi_{A} = 5\sin 70^{\circ} = 5(0.9397) = 4.698
$$

$$
z_{A} = -3
$$

For $B$:

$$
x_{B} = \rho_{B}\cos\phi_{B} = 2\cos(-30^{\circ}) = 2(0.8660) = 1.732
$$

$$
y_{B} = \rho_{B}\sin\phi_{B} = 2\sin(-30^{\circ}) = 2(-0.5) = -1.000
$$

$$
z_{B} = 1
$$

**Step 2 — (a) Distance vector and its unit vector in Cartesian form**

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{R}_{AB} &= (x_{B}-x_{A})\hat{a}_{x}+(y_{B}-y_{A})\hat{a}_{y}+(z_{B}-z_{A})\hat{a}_{z} \\
&= (1.732-1.710)\hat{a}_{x}+(-1.000-4.698)\hat{a}_{y}+(1-(-3))\hat{a}_{z} \\
&= 0.022\hat{a}_{x}-5.698\hat{a}_{y}+4.000\hat{a}_{z}
\end{align*}
$$

$$
|\mathbf{R}_{AB}| = \sqrt{(0.022)^{2}+(-5.698)^{2}+(4.000)^{2}} = \sqrt{0.0005+32.467+16} = \sqrt{48.467} = 6.962
$$

$$
\hat{a}_{AB} = \frac{\mathbf{R}_{AB}}{|\mathbf{R}_{AB}|} = \frac{0.022\hat{a}_{x}-5.698\hat{a}_{y}+4.000\hat{a}_{z}}{6.962}
= 0.003\hat{a}_{x}-0.818\hat{a}_{y}+0.575\hat{a}_{z}
$$

**Step 3 — (b) Same unit vector expressed in cylindrical components at $A$**

The transformation must use the angle of the point at which the vector is expressed, i.e. $\phi_{A}=70^{\circ}$, so $\cos\phi_{A}=0.3420$ and $\sin\phi_{A}=0.9397$. Applying (B) to $\mathbf{R}_{AB}$:

$$
R_{\rho} = R_{x}\cos\phi_{A}+R_{y}\sin\phi_{A} = (0.022)(0.3420)+(-5.698)(0.9397) = 0.008-5.354 = -5.346
$$

$$
R_{\phi} = -R_{x}\sin\phi_{A}+R_{y}\cos\phi_{A} = -(0.022)(0.9397)+(-5.698)(0.3420) = -0.021-1.949 = -1.970
$$

$$
R_{z} = 4.000
$$

Check:

$$
\sqrt{(-5.346)^{2}+(-1.970)^{2}+4^{2}} = \sqrt{28.58+3.88+16} = \sqrt{48.46} = 6.962\ \checkmark
$$

Dividing by the magnitude:

$$
\hat{a}_{AB} = \frac{-5.346\hat{a}_{\rho}-1.970\hat{a}_{\phi}+4.000\hat{a}_{z}}{6.962}
= -0.768\hat{a}_{\rho}-0.283\hat{a}_{\phi}+0.575\hat{a}_{z}
$$

questions.text: Express in Cartesian components: (a) the vector at $A(\rho=4,\ \Phi=40^{\circ},\ z=-2)$ that extends to $B(\rho=5,\ \Phi=-110^{\circ},\ z=2)$; and (b) a unit vector at $B$ directed toward $A$.

Define a vector field. A field vector is given by

$$
\mathbf{A} = \frac{x\hat{a}_{x}+y\hat{a}_{y}+z\hat{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}};
$$

transform this vector into the cylindrical coordinate system at the point $(2,30^{\circ},6)$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Definition of a vector field**

A vector field is a function that assigns a vector quantity — having both a magnitude and a direction — to every point of a region of space. In general it is written $\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{A}(x,y,z)$, meaning that both the magnitude and direction may change from point to point. Examples include the electric field intensity $\mathbf{E}$, the magnetic field intensity $\mathbf{H}$ and the velocity field of a fluid. This is in contrast to a scalar field (such as potential $V$ or temperature $T$), which assigns only a magnitude to each point.

**Step 2 — Recognise the given field**

Note that $x\hat{a}_{x}+y\hat{a}_{y}+z\hat{a}_{z}=\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector and $\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}=r=|\mathbf{r}|$. Hence

$$
\mathbf{A} = \frac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}|} = \hat{a}_{r},
$$

i.e. the given field is simply the unit radial vector of the spherical system, which has unit magnitude everywhere.

**Step 3 — General transformation to cylindrical components**

In cylindrical variables, $x=\rho\cos\phi$, $y=\rho\sin\phi$, and $\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}=\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}$. Thus the Cartesian components are

$$
A_{x} = \frac{\rho\cos\phi}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}},\qquad
A_{y} = \frac{\rho\sin\phi}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}},\qquad
A_{z} = \frac{z}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}}
$$

Applying (B):

$$
A_{\rho} = A_{x}\cos\phi+A_{y}\sin\phi = \frac{\rho\cos^{2}\phi}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}}+\frac{\rho\sin^{2}\phi}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}} = \frac{\rho}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}}
$$

$$
A_{\phi} = -A_{x}\sin\phi+A_{y}\cos\phi = \frac{-\rho\cos\phi\sin\phi+\rho\sin\phi\cos\phi}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}} = 0
$$

$$
A_{z} = \frac{z}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}}
$$

Therefore, in general:

$$
\mathbf{A} = \frac{\rho}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}}\,\hat{a}_{\rho} + \frac{z}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}}\,\hat{a}_{z}
$$

**Step 4 — Evaluate at $(\rho=2,\ \phi=30^{\circ},\ z=6)$**

$$
\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}} = \sqrt{2^{2}+6^{2}} = \sqrt{4+36} = \sqrt{40} = 6.325
$$

$$
A_{\rho} = \frac{2}{6.325} = 0.316,\qquad
A_{\phi} = 0,\qquad
A_{z} = \frac{6}{6.325} = 0.949
$$

**Step 5 — Verification**

$$
|\mathbf{A}| = \sqrt{(0.316)^{2}+(0.949)^{2}} = \sqrt{0.0999+0.9006} = \sqrt{1.0005}\approx 1\ \checkmark
$$

which is correct, since $\mathbf{A}=\hat{a}_{r}$ is a unit vector.

questions.text: Transform $\mathbf{A}_{c}=x\hat{a}_{x}+xy\hat{a}_{z}$ at the point $(1,2,3)$ from the Cartesian to the cylindrical coordinate system.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Evaluate the components at the given point**

At $(x,y,z)=(1,2,3)$:

$$
A_{x} = x = 1,\qquad
A_{y} = 0,\qquad
A_{z} = xy = (1)(2) = 2
$$

**Step 2 — Cylindrical coordinates of the point**

$$
\rho = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} = \sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}} = \sqrt{5} = 2.236
$$

$x=1>0$, $y=2>0$ ⇒ first quadrant:

$$
\phi = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{2}{1} = 63.43^{\circ},\qquad z=3
$$

$$
\cos\phi = \frac{1}{2.236} = 0.4472,\qquad
\sin\phi = \frac{2}{2.236} = 0.8944
$$

**Step 3 — Transform using (B)**

$$
A_{\rho} = A_{x}\cos\phi+A_{y}\sin\phi = (1)(0.4472)+0 = 0.447
$$

$$
A_{\phi} = -A_{x}\sin\phi+A_{y}\cos\phi = -(1)(0.8944)+0 = -0.894
$$

$$
A_{z} = 2
$$

**Step 4 — General form (for completeness)**

Substituting $A_{x}=x=\rho\cos\phi$ and $A_{z}=xy=\rho^{2}\sin\phi\cos\phi$:

$$
\mathbf{A}_{c} = \rho\cos^{2}\phi\,\hat{a}_{\rho} - \rho\sin\phi\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi} + \rho^{2}\sin\phi\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{z}
$$

Checking at $\rho=2.236$, $\phi=63.43^{\circ}$:

$$
\rho\cos^{2}\phi = 2.236(0.4472)^{2} = 2.236(0.2) = 0.447\ \checkmark
$$

$$
\rho^{2}\sin\phi\cos\phi = 5(0.8944)(0.4472) = 2\ \checkmark
$$

**Step 5 — Verification**

$$
\sqrt{(0.447)^{2}+(-0.894)^{2}+2^{2}} = \sqrt{0.200+0.799+4} = \sqrt{4.999} = 2.236
$$

$$
\sqrt{1^{2}+0^{2}+2^{2}} = \sqrt{5} = 2.236\ \checkmark
$$

questions.text: (a) Transform a point $(x,y,z)$ in rectangular coordinates to a point $(r,\theta,\phi)$ in spherical coordinates and vice-versa. (b) Transform $\mathbf{B}=y\hat{a}_{x}-x\hat{a}_{y}+z\hat{a}_{z}$ into cylindrical coordinates.
questions.solution:
**Part (a) — Rectangular → Spherical**

Consider a point $P(x,y,z)$ with position vector $\mathbf{r}$. From the geometry of the spherical system:

(i) Radial distance $r$ — the straight-line distance from the origin to $P$. By applying Pythagoras’ theorem twice (first in the $xy$-plane to get $\rho=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$, then in the vertical plane containing $\mathbf{r}$ and the $z$-axis):

$$
r = \sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}} = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}},\qquad 0\le r<\infty
$$

(ii) Polar angle $\theta$ — measured from the positive $z$-axis down to $\mathbf{r}$. Since $z=r\cos\theta$ and $\rho=r\sin\theta$:

$$
\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\frac{z}{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}} = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}}{z},\qquad 0\le\theta\le 180^{\circ}
$$

(iii) Azimuthal angle $\phi$ — measured in the $xy$-plane from the positive $x$-axis:

$$
\phi = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{y}{x},\qquad 0\le\phi\le 360^{\circ}
$$

**Spherical → Rectangular:** projecting $\mathbf{r}$ onto the $xy$-plane gives $\rho=r\sin\theta$; resolving $\rho$ along $x$ and $y$, and taking the $z$-projection directly:

$$
x = r\sin\theta\cos\phi,\qquad
y = r\sin\theta\sin\phi,\qquad
z = r\cos\theta
$$

**Part (b) — Transform $\mathbf{B}=y\hat{a}_{x}-x\hat{a}_{y}+z\hat{a}_{z}$**

Substituting $x=\rho\cos\phi$ and $y=\rho\sin\phi$, the Cartesian components become:

$$
B_{x} = y = \rho\sin\phi,\qquad
B_{y} = -x = -\rho\cos\phi,\qquad
B_{z} = z
$$

Applying (B):

$$
B_{\rho} = B_{x}\cos\phi+B_{y}\sin\phi = \rho\sin\phi\cos\phi-\rho\cos\phi\sin\phi = 0
$$

$$
B_{\phi} = -B_{x}\sin\phi+B_{y}\cos\phi = -\rho\sin^{2}\phi-\rho\cos^{2}\phi = -\rho(\sin^{2}\phi+\cos^{2}\phi) = -\rho
$$

$$
B_{z} = z
$$

**Interpretation**

$B_{\rho}=0$ means the field has no radial component — it circulates about the $z$-axis with magnitude proportional to $\rho$, in the $-\hat{a}_{\phi}$ sense. This is precisely the form of the field of a rigid rotation about the $z$-axis.

questions.text: Express the uniform vector field $\mathbf{F}=5\hat{a}_{x}$ in (a) cylindrical and (b) spherical components.
questions.solution:
Here $F_{x}=5$, $F_{y}=0$, $F_{z}=0$ everywhere (a uniform field: constant magnitude and direction at every point).

**Part (a) — Cylindrical components**

Applying (B):

$$
F_{\rho} = F_{x}\cos\phi+F_{y}\sin\phi = 5\cos\phi
$$

$$
F_{\phi} = -F_{x}\sin\phi+F_{y}\cos\phi = -5\sin\phi
$$

$$
F_{z} = 0
$$

$$
\mathbf{F} = 5\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{\rho}-5\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi}
$$

**Part (b) — Spherical components**

Applying (E):

$$
F_{r} = F_{x}\sin\theta\cos\phi+F_{y}\sin\theta\sin\phi+F_{z}\cos\theta = 5\sin\theta\cos\phi
$$

$$
F_{\theta} = F_{x}\cos\theta\cos\phi+F_{y}\cos\theta\sin\phi-F_{z}\sin\theta = 5\cos\theta\cos\phi
$$

$$
F_{\phi} = -F_{x}\sin\phi+F_{y}\cos\phi = -5\sin\phi
$$

$$
\mathbf{F} = 5\sin\theta\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{r}+5\cos\theta\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{\theta}-5\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi}
$$

**Verification**

Cylindrical:

$$
|\mathbf{F}| = \sqrt{25\cos^{2}\phi+25\sin^{2}\phi} = \sqrt{25} = 5\ \checkmark
$$

Spherical:

$$
\begin{align*}
|\mathbf{F}|^{2} &= 25\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\phi + 25\cos^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\phi + 25\sin^{2}\phi \\
&= 25\cos^{2}\phi(\sin^{2}\theta+\cos^{2}\theta)+25\sin^{2}\phi \\
&= 25\cos^{2}\phi+25\sin^{2}\phi = 25
\end{align*}
$$

so $|\mathbf{F}|=5\ \checkmark$

**Important observation**

Although the field is uniform, its components in the cylindrical and spherical systems are functions of position ($\phi$ and $\theta$). This is because $\hat{a}_{\rho}$, $\hat{a}_{\phi}$, $\hat{a}_{r}$ and $\hat{a}_{\theta}$ themselves change direction from point to point, unlike the fixed Cartesian unit vectors.

questions.text: Express the vector field $\mathbf{W}=(x-y)\hat{a}_{y}$ in cylindrical and spherical coordinates.
questions.solution:
Here $W_{x}=0$, $W_{y}=(x-y)$, $W_{z}=0$.

**Part (a) — Cylindrical coordinates**

Substituting $x=\rho\cos\phi$, $y=\rho\sin\phi$:

$$
W_{y} = x-y = \rho\cos\phi-\rho\sin\phi = \rho(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)
$$

Applying (B):

$$
W_{\rho} = W_{x}\cos\phi+W_{y}\sin\phi = \rho(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)\sin\phi = \rho\sin\phi(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)
$$

$$
W_{\phi} = -W_{x}\sin\phi+W_{y}\cos\phi = \rho(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)\cos\phi = \rho\cos\phi(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)
$$

$$
W_{z} = 0
$$

$$
\mathbf{W} = \rho(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)\bigl(\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{\rho}+\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi}\bigr)
$$

**Part (b) — Spherical coordinates**

Substituting $x=r\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=r\sin\theta\sin\phi$:

$$
W_{y} = x-y = r\sin\theta\cos\phi-r\sin\theta\sin\phi = r\sin\theta(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)
$$

Applying (E) with $W_{x}=W_{z}=0$:

$$
W_{r} = W_{y}\sin\theta\sin\phi = r\sin^{2}\theta\sin\phi(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)
$$

$$
W_{\theta} = W_{y}\cos\theta\sin\phi = r\sin\theta\cos\theta\sin\phi(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)
$$

$$
W_{\phi} = W_{y}\cos\phi = r\sin\theta\cos\phi(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)
$$

$$
\mathbf{W} = r\sin\theta(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)\bigl(\sin\theta\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{r}+\cos\theta\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{\theta}+\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{\phi}\bigr)
$$

**Verification (cylindrical)**

$$
|\mathbf{W}|^{2} = \rho^{2}(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)^{2}(\sin^{2}\phi+\cos^{2}\phi) = \rho^{2}(\cos\phi-\sin\phi)^{2}
$$

so $|\mathbf{W}|=\rho|\cos\phi-\sin\phi|=|x-y|$, which matches the Cartesian magnitude $|\mathbf{W}|=|x-y|\ \checkmark$

questions.text: Convert the vector $\mathbf{F}=F_{x}\hat{a}_{x}+F_{y}\hat{a}_{y}+F_{z}\hat{a}_{z}$ into the spherical coordinate system.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Principle**

The component of $\mathbf{F}$ along any direction $\hat{a}_{u}$ is obtained by the dot product $F_{u}=\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{a}_{u}$. Hence:

$$
F_{r} = \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{a}_{r},\qquad
F_{\theta} = \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{a}_{\theta},\qquad
F_{\phi} = \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{a}_{\phi}
$$

**Step 2 — Dot products of the unit vectors**

The spherical unit vectors expressed in Cartesian form are:

$$
\hat{a}_{r} = \sin\theta\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{x}+\sin\theta\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{y}+\cos\theta\,\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
\hat{a}_{\theta} = \cos\theta\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{x}+\cos\theta\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{y}-\sin\theta\,\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
\hat{a}_{\phi} = -\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{x}+\cos\phi\,\hat{a}_{y}
$$

This gives the standard dot-product table:

|  | $\hat{a}_{x}$ | $\hat{a}_{y}$ | $\hat{a}_{z}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\hat{a}_{r}$ | $\sin\theta\cos\phi$ | $\sin\theta\sin\phi$ | $\cos\theta$ |
| $\hat{a}_{\theta}$ | $\cos\theta\cos\phi$ | $\cos\theta\sin\phi$ | $-\sin\theta$ |
| $\hat{a}_{\phi}$ | $-\sin\phi$ | $\cos\phi$ | $0$ |

**Step 3 — Form the components**

$$
\begin{align*}
F_{r} &= \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{a}_{r} = F_{x}(\hat{a}_{x}\cdot\hat{a}_{r})+F_{y}(\hat{a}_{y}\cdot\hat{a}_{r})+F_{z}(\hat{a}_{z}\cdot\hat{a}_{r}) \\
&= F_{x}\sin\theta\cos\phi + F_{y}\sin\theta\sin\phi + F_{z}\cos\theta
\end{align*}
$$

$$
F_{\theta} = \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{a}_{\theta} = F_{x}\cos\theta\cos\phi + F_{y}\cos\theta\sin\phi - F_{z}\sin\theta
$$

$$
F_{\phi} = \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{a}_{\phi} = -F_{x}\sin\phi + F_{y}\cos\phi
$$

**Step 4 — Matrix form**

$$
\begin{bmatrix} F_{r} \\ F_{\theta} \\ F_{\phi} \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sin\theta\cos\phi & \sin\theta\sin\phi & \cos\theta \\
\cos\theta\cos\phi & \cos\theta\sin\phi & -\sin\theta \\
-\sin\phi & \cos\phi & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} F_{x} \\ F_{y} \\ F_{z} \end{bmatrix}
$$

The transformation matrix is orthogonal (its inverse equals its transpose), which is why $|\mathbf{F}|$ is preserved.

questions.text: Transform $\mathbf{A}=\rho\sin\phi\,\hat{a}_{z}$ at the point $(1,45^{\circ},2)$ from the cylindrical to the spherical coordinate system.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Evaluate the field at the given point**

At $(\rho,\phi,z)=(1,45^{\circ},2)$:

$$
A_{z} = \rho\sin\phi = (1)\sin 45^{\circ} = 0.7071
$$

So at this point $\mathbf{A}=0.7071\hat{a}_{z}$, with $A_{\rho}=A_{\phi}=0$.

**Step 2 — Convert the point to spherical coordinates**

$$
r = \sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}} = \sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}} = \sqrt{5} = 2.236
$$

$$
\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{\rho}{z} = \tan^{-1}\!\frac{1}{2} = 26.57^{\circ},\qquad
\phi = 45^{\circ}\ \text{(unchanged)}
$$

$$
\sin\theta = \frac{\rho}{r} = \frac{1}{2.236} = 0.4472,\qquad
\cos\theta = \frac{z}{r} = \frac{2}{2.236} = 0.8944
$$

**Step 3 — Resolve $\hat{a}_{z}$ into spherical unit vectors**

From relation (F):

$$
\hat{a}_{z} = \cos\theta\,\hat{a}_{r}-\sin\theta\,\hat{a}_{\theta}
$$

Therefore:

$$
A_{r} = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\qquad
A_{\theta} = -\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\qquad
A_{\phi} = 0
$$

giving the general result:

$$
\mathbf{A} = A_{z}\hat{a}_{z} = \rho\sin\phi\bigl(\cos\theta\,\hat{a}_{r}-\sin\theta\,\hat{a}_{\theta}\bigr)
$$

**Step 4 — Substitute the numerical values**

$$
A_{r} = (0.7071)(0.8944) = 0.632
$$

$$
A_{\theta} = -(0.7071)(0.4472) = -0.316
$$

$$
A_{\phi} = 0
$$

**Step 5 — Verification**

$$
|\mathbf{A}| = \sqrt{(0.632)^{2}+(-0.316)^{2}} = \sqrt{0.399+0.0999} = \sqrt{0.499} = 0.707\ \checkmark
$$

which equals the original magnitude $|A_{z}|=0.7071$.

questions.text: A point charge of $12\,\mathrm{nC}$ is located at the origin. Four uniform line charges lie in the $x=0$ plane as follows: $80\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ at $y=-1$ and $-5\,\mathrm{m}$, and $-50\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ at $y=-2$ and $-4\,\mathrm{m}$. Find the electric flux density $\mathbf{D}$ at $P(0,-3,2)$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Establish the geometry**

The four line charges lie in the plane $x=0$. Within that plane the free coordinates are $y$ and $z$; specifying only a value of $y$ therefore defines a straight line parallel to the $z$-axis:

| Line | Location | Density | Direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| $L_{1}$ | $x=0$, $y=-1$ | $\rho_{L1}=+80\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ | $\parallel z$ |
| $L_{2}$ | $x=0$, $y=-5$ | $\rho_{L2}=+80\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ | $\parallel z$ |
| $L_{3}$ | $x=0$, $y=-2$ | $\rho_{L3}=-50\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ | $\parallel z$ |
| $L_{4}$ | $x=0$, $y=-4$ | $\rho_{L4}=-50\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ | $\parallel z$ |

The field point is $P(0,-3,2)$.

**Step 2 — Contribution of the point charge at the origin**

$$
\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{r}_{P}-\mathbf{r}_{Q}
= (-3)\hat{a}_{y}+2\hat{a}_{z},\qquad
|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}=3.606\,\mathrm{m}
$$

$$
\hat{a}_{R}=\frac{-3\hat{a}_{y}+2\hat{a}_{z}}{3.606}
=-0.8321\hat{a}_{y}+0.5547\hat{a}_{z}
$$

Using $\mathbf{D}=Q/(4\pi R^{2})\,\hat{a}_{R}$ with $R^{2}=13$:

$$
\frac{Q}{4\pi R^{2}}
= \frac{12\times 10^{-9}}{4\pi(13)}
= 7.346\times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
= 0.07346\,\mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{Q}
= 0.07346\bigl(-0.8321\hat{a}_{y}+0.5547\hat{a}_{z}\bigr)
= -0.0611\hat{a}_{y}+0.0407\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

**Step 3 — Contribution of $L_{1}$ ($y=-1$) and $L_{2}$ ($y=-5$)**

For a line parallel to the $z$-axis, the perpendicular distance is measured in the $xy$-plane only.

Line $L_{1}$ at $(x=0,\,y=-1)$:

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}_{1}=-2\hat{a}_{y},\quad \rho_{1}=2\,\mathrm{m},\quad \hat{a}_{\rho_{1}}=-\hat{a}_{y}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{1}
= \frac{\rho_{L1}}{2\pi\rho_{1}}\,\hat{a}_{\rho_{1}}
= \frac{80\times 10^{-9}}{2\pi(2)}(-\hat{a}_{y})
= -6.366\hat{a}_{y}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

Line $L_{2}$ at $(x=0,\,y=-5)$:

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}_{2}=+2\hat{a}_{y},\quad \rho_{2}=2\,\mathrm{m},\quad \hat{a}_{\rho_{2}}=+\hat{a}_{y}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{2}
= \frac{80\times 10^{-9}}{2\pi(2)}(+\hat{a}_{y})
= +6.366\hat{a}_{y}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\therefore\ \mathbf{D}_{1}+\mathbf{D}_{2}=0
$$

**Step 4 — Contribution of $L_{3}$ ($y=-2$) and $L_{4}$ ($y=-4$)**

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}_{3}=-\hat{a}_{y},\quad \rho_{3}=1\,\mathrm{m},\quad \hat{a}_{\rho_{3}}=-\hat{a}_{y}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{3}
= \frac{-50\times 10^{-9}}{2\pi(1)}(-\hat{a}_{y})
= +7.958\hat{a}_{y}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}_{4}=+\hat{a}_{y},\quad \rho_{4}=1\,\mathrm{m},\quad \hat{a}_{\rho_{4}}=+\hat{a}_{y}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{4}
= \frac{-50\times 10^{-9}}{2\pi(1)}(+\hat{a}_{y})
= -7.958\hat{a}_{y}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\therefore\ \mathbf{D}_{3}+\mathbf{D}_{4}=0
$$

**Step 5 — Why the lines cancel (the key insight)**

The field point lies at $y=-3$. The pair $L_{1}$, $L_{2}$ sits at $y=-1$ and $y=-5$ — symmetrically $2\,\mathrm{m}$ on either side of $P$, with equal densities — so their fields cancel exactly. The pair $L_{3}$, $L_{4}$ at $y=-2$ and $y=-4$ is likewise symmetric about $y=-3$ at $1\,\mathrm{m}$ each side, and also cancels. Only the point charge contributes.

**Step 6 — Total flux density**

$$
\mathbf{D}=\mathbf{D}_{Q}=-0.0611\hat{a}_{y}+0.0407\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

Magnitude check:

$$
|\mathbf{D}|=\sqrt{(0.0611)^{2}+(0.0407)^{2}}=\sqrt{0.005389}=0.0734\,\mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

which agrees with $Q/(4\pi R^{2})=0.0735\,\mathrm{nC/m^{2}}$ found in Step 2.

questions.text: A point charge of $6\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ is at the origin, a uniform line charge density of $180\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ lies along the $x$-axis, and a uniform sheet charge of $25\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}$ lies on the $z=0$ plane. Find $\mathbf{D}$ at the point $(1,2,4)$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Contribution of the point charge $Q=6\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ at the origin**

$$
\mathbf{R}=\hat{a}_{x}+2\hat{a}_{y}+4\hat{a}_{z},\qquad
|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{21}=4.583\,\mathrm{m},\qquad R^{2}=21
$$

$$
\hat{a}_{R}=0.2182\hat{a}_{x}+0.4364\hat{a}_{y}+0.8729\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
\frac{Q}{4\pi R^{2}}
= \frac{6\times 10^{-6}}{4\pi(21)}
= 2.274\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{Q}
= 4.96\hat{a}_{x}+9.92\hat{a}_{y}+19.85\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

**Step 2 — Contribution of the line charge along the $x$-axis**

Perpendicular distance in the $yz$-plane only:

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}=2\hat{a}_{y}+4\hat{a}_{z},\qquad
\rho=\sqrt{20}=4.472\,\mathrm{m}
$$

$$
\hat{a}_{\rho}=0.4472\hat{a}_{y}+0.8944\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\rho}
= \frac{180\times 10^{-9}}{2\pi(4.472)}
= 6.406\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{L}=2.87\hat{a}_{y}+5.73\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

**Step 3 — Contribution of the sheet charge on the $z=0$ plane**

The field point has $z=4>0$, so $\hat{a}_{N}=+\hat{a}_{z}$:

$$
\mathbf{D}_{S}=\frac{\rho_{S}}{2}\,\hat{a}_{N}=\frac{25}{2}\hat{a}_{z}=12.5\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

**Step 4 — Total**

$$
D_{x}=4.96\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}},\qquad
D_{y}=1.279\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}},\qquad
D_{z}\approx 12.5\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}\approx 4.96\times 10^{-9}\hat{a}_{x}+1.279\times 10^{-8}\hat{a}_{y}+12.5\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

**Step 5 — Remark on the magnitudes**

Taken literally, $\rho_{S}=25\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}$ is enormous: it produces $12.5\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}$, about nine orders of magnitude larger than the point- and line-charge terms. The answer is then dominated by the sheet.

If, as the surrounding data strongly suggest, the intended density is $\rho_{S}=25\,\mathrm{nC/m^{2}}$, then $\mathbf{D}_{S}=12.5\hat{a}_{z}\,\mathrm{nC/m^{2}}$ and

$$
\mathbf{D}=4.96\hat{a}_{x}+12.79\hat{a}_{y}+38.08\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

Both results are given below; state your assumption clearly in the examination.

questions.text: Find $\mathbf{D}$ at $P(6,8,10)$ caused by a point charge $30\,\mathrm{nC}$ at the origin, a uniform line charge $\rho_{L}=40\,\mu\mathrm{C/m}$ on the $z$-axis, and a uniform surface charge density $\rho_{S}=57.2\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}}$ on the plane $x=9$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Point charge $Q=30\,\mathrm{nC}$ at the origin**

$$
\mathbf{R}=6\hat{a}_{x}+8\hat{a}_{y}+10\hat{a}_{z},\qquad
|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{200}=14.142\,\mathrm{m},\qquad R^{2}=200
$$

$$
\hat{a}_{R}=0.4243\hat{a}_{x}+0.5657\hat{a}_{y}+0.7071\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
\frac{Q}{4\pi R^{2}}
= \frac{30\times 10^{-9}}{4\pi(200)}
= 1.194\times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{Q}
= 0.00507\hat{a}_{x}+0.00675\hat{a}_{y}+0.00844\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{nC/m^{2}}
$$

This contribution is negligible compared with the others.

**Step 2 — Line charge $\rho_{L}=40\,\mu\mathrm{C/m}$ on the $z$-axis**

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}=6\hat{a}_{x}+8\hat{a}_{y},\qquad
\rho=10\,\mathrm{m},\qquad
\hat{a}_{\rho}=0.6\hat{a}_{x}+0.8\hat{a}_{y}
$$

$$
\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\rho}
= \frac{40\times 10^{-6}}{2\pi(10)}
= 6.366\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

$$
\mathbf{D}_{L}=0.382\hat{a}_{x}+0.509\hat{a}_{y}\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

**Step 3 — Sheet charge $\rho_{S}=57.2\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}}$ on the plane $x=9$**

The field point has $x=6<9$, so $\hat{a}_{N}=-\hat{a}_{x}$:

$$
\mathbf{D}_{S}=\frac{\rho_{S}}{2}\,\hat{a}_{N}=-28.6\hat{a}_{x}\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

**Step 4 — Superpose all three contributions**

Working in $\mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}}$ ($\mathbf{D}_{Q}$ entirely negligible):

$$
D_{x}=-28.218\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}},\qquad
D_{y}=0.509\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}},\qquad
D_{z}\approx 0
$$

**Step 5 — Result and magnitude**

$$
\mathbf{D}\approx -28.22\hat{a}_{x}+0.51\hat{a}_{y}\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}},\qquad
|\mathbf{D}|=28.22\,\mu\mathrm{C/m^{2}}
$$

The sheet charge dominates: its field does not decay with distance.

questions.text: An infinite uniform line charge $\rho_{L}=2\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ lies along the $x$-axis, while point charges of $8\,\mathrm{nC}$ each are located at $(0,0,1)$ and $(0,0,-1)$. Find $\mathbf{D}$ at $(2,3,-4)$.

State Coulomb’s law. Derive an expression for the electric field intensity of an infinite line charge of uniform density $\rho_{L}$ using Coulomb’s law. A uniform line charge of $20\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ is located at $y=3$, $z=5$; find $\mathbf{E}$ at $P(5,6,1)$.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Statement of Coulomb’s law**

Coulomb’s law states that the force between two point charges $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ is:
- directly proportional to the product of the charges, $Q_{1}Q_{2}$;
- inversely proportional to the square of the distance $R$ between them;
- directed along the straight line joining the two charges;
- repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike charges.

Mathematically:

$$
F=\frac{kQ_{1}Q_{2}}{R^{2}},\qquad
k=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}=9\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{m/F}
$$

In vector form, the force on $Q_{2}$ due to $Q_{1}$ is

$$
\mathbf{F}_{12}=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}\,\hat{a}_{R_{12}}
$$

where $\hat{a}_{R_{12}}$ is the unit vector directed from $Q_{1}$ to $Q_{2}$. The electric field intensity is the force per unit positive test charge:

$$
\mathbf{E}=\frac{\mathbf{F}}{Q_{t}}=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}\,\hat{a}_{R}\ \mathrm{V/m}
$$

**Part 2 — Derivation of $\mathbf{E}$ for an infinite line charge**

*Set-up.* Let the line charge of uniform density $\rho_{L}$ (C/m) lie along the $z$-axis, extending from $z=-\infty$ to $z=+\infty$. By symmetry, take the field point $P$ in the $z=0$ plane at a perpendicular distance $\rho$ from the line, i.e. $P(\rho,0,0)$.

*Elemental charge.* An element of length $dz$ at height $z$ carries $dQ=\rho_{L}\,dz$.

*Distance and direction.* The vector from the element at $(0,0,z)$ to $P(\rho,0,0)$ is

$$
\mathbf{R}=\rho\hat{a}_{\rho}-z\hat{a}_{z},\qquad
|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}},\qquad
\hat{a}_{R}=\frac{\rho\hat{a}_{\rho}-z\hat{a}_{z}}{\sqrt{\rho^{2}+z^{2}}}
$$

*Elemental field (Coulomb’s law).*

$$
d\mathbf{E}
= \frac{\rho_{L}\,dz}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}(\rho^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}\bigl(\rho\hat{a}_{\rho}-z\hat{a}_{z}\bigr)
$$

*Symmetry.* For every element at $+z$ there is an identical element at $-z$. Their $\hat{a}_{z}$-components cancel in pairs, while their $\hat{a}_{\rho}$-components add. Hence $E_{z}=0$ and

$$
E_{\rho}
= \frac{\rho_{L}\rho}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(\rho^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}
$$

*Evaluating the integral.* Substitute $z=\rho\tan\alpha$, so $dz=\rho\sec^{2}\alpha\,d\alpha$ and $\rho^{2}+z^{2}=\rho^{2}\sec^{2}\alpha$. Limits $z=-\infty\to+\infty$ become $\alpha=-\pi/2\to+\pi/2$:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(\rho^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}
= \frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos\alpha\,d\alpha
= \frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\bigl[\sin\alpha\bigr]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}
= \frac{2}{\rho^{2}}
$$

*Result.*

$$
E_{\rho}=\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}\rho},\qquad
\mathbf{E}=\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}\rho}\,\hat{a}_{\rho}\ \mathrm{V/m}
$$

The field falls off as $1/\rho$ (not $1/\rho^{2}$) and is directed radially away from the line for $\rho_{L}>0$.

**Part 3 — Numerical problem**

The line is specified by $y=3$, $z=5$ with $x$ unrestricted, so it is parallel to the $x$-axis. The $x$-coordinate of $P(5,6,1)$ is irrelevant:

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}=3\hat{a}_{y}-4\hat{a}_{z},\qquad
\rho=5\,\mathrm{m},\qquad
\hat{a}_{\rho}=0.6\hat{a}_{y}-0.8\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
E=\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}\rho}
= \frac{20\times 10^{-9}}{2\pi(8.854\times 10^{-12})(5)}
= 71.89\,\mathrm{V/m}
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}=71.89\bigl(0.6\hat{a}_{y}-0.8\hat{a}_{z}\bigr)
= 43.13\hat{a}_{y}-57.51\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{V/m}
$$

Check: $|\mathbf{E}|=\sqrt{(43.13)^{2}+(57.51)^{2}}=71.89\,\mathrm{V/m}$ $\checkmark$

questions.text: Derive the expression for electric field intensity due to an infinite line charge using Gauss’s law.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Statement of Gauss’s law**

$$
\Psi=\oint_{S}\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}
$$

**Step 2 — Choice of the Gaussian surface**

Let an infinite line charge of uniform density $\rho_{L}$ (C/m) lie along the $z$-axis. By symmetry:
- $\mathbf{D}$ must be directed radially, $\mathbf{D}=D_{\rho}\hat{a}_{\rho}$;
- $D_{\rho}$ can depend only on $\rho$.

Choose a closed right circular cylinder of radius $\rho$ and length $L$, coaxial with the line charge.

**Step 3 — Evaluate the flux integral over the three surfaces**

Top and bottom caps: $d\mathbf{S}=\pm dS\,\hat{a}_{z}$, while $\mathbf{D}=D_{\rho}\hat{a}_{\rho}$, so $\hat{a}_{\rho}\cdot\hat{a}_{z}=0$ and those contributions vanish.

Curved side: $d\mathbf{S}=dS\,\hat{a}_{\rho}$, and $D_{\rho}$ is constant on the surface:

$$
\int_{\mathrm{side}}\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=D_{\rho}(2\pi\rho L)
$$

**Step 4 — Charge enclosed**

$$
Q_{\mathrm{enc}}=\rho_{L}L
$$

**Step 5 — Apply Gauss’s law and solve**

$$
D_{\rho}(2\pi\rho L)=\rho_{L}L
\implies
D_{\rho}=\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\rho}
$$

Since $\mathbf{D}=\varepsilon_{0}\mathbf{E}$ in free space:

$$
\mathbf{D}=\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\rho}\,\hat{a}_{\rho}\ \mathrm{C/m^{2}},\qquad
\mathbf{E}=\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}\rho}\,\hat{a}_{\rho}\ \mathrm{V/m}
$$

**Step 6 — Observations**

The length $L$ cancels, as it must. The field varies as $1/\rho$. Compare with the Coulomb’s-law derivation (Question 5): Gauss’s law gives the same result in a few lines without source integration, because the symmetry was exploited at the outset — but it works only when the charge distribution is symmetric enough for $\mathbf{D}$ to be taken outside the integral.
questions.answer: $\boxed{\mathbf{E}=\dfrac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}\rho}\,\hat{a}_{\rho}\ \mathrm{V/m},\ \text{directed radially away from the line for }\rho_{L}>0}$

questions.text: State Coulomb’s law with an example. An infinitely long uniform line charge is located at $y=3$, $z=5$ with $\rho_{L}=30\,\mathrm{nC/m}$; find $\mathbf{E}$ at $P_{A}(0,0,0)$, $P_{B}(0,6,1)$ and $P_{C}(5,6,1)$.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Coulomb’s law with an example**

*Statement.* The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining them:

$$
\mathbf{F}=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}}\,\hat{a}_{R}
$$

*Example.* Two point charges $Q_{1}=+1\,\mathrm{mC}$ and $Q_{2}=-2\,\mathrm{mC}$ are separated by $R=3\,\mathrm{m}$ in free space:

$$
F=\frac{(9\times 10^{9})(1\times 10^{-3})(2\times 10^{-3})}{3^{2}}=2\times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{N}=2\,\mathrm{kN}
$$

Since the charges are of opposite sign, the force is attractive.

**Part 2 — Common set-up for the three field points**

The line is parallel to the $x$-axis ($y=3$, $z=5$, $x$ free). The $x$-coordinate of any field point is irrelevant. Evaluate the constant factor once:

$$
\frac{\rho_{L}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}}
= \frac{30\times 10^{-9}}{2\pi(8.854\times 10^{-12})}
= 539.3\,\mathrm{V}
$$

so that $\mathbf{E}=(539.3/\rho)\,\hat{a}_{\rho}\ \mathrm{V/m}$ in every case.

**Part 3(a) — Field at $P_{A}(0,0,0)$**

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}_{A}=-3\hat{a}_{y}-5\hat{a}_{z},\qquad
\rho_{A}=\sqrt{34}=5.831\,\mathrm{m}
$$

$$
\hat{a}_{\rho_{A}}=-0.5145\hat{a}_{y}-0.8575\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
E_{A}=\frac{539.3}{5.831}=92.49\,\mathrm{V/m}
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{A}=-47.58\hat{a}_{y}-79.31\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{V/m}
$$

**Part 3(b) — Field at $P_{B}(0,6,1)$**

$$
\boldsymbol{\rho}_{B}=3\hat{a}_{y}-4\hat{a}_{z},\qquad
\rho_{B}=5\,\mathrm{m},\qquad
\hat{a}_{\rho_{B}}=0.6\hat{a}_{y}-0.8\hat{a}_{z}
$$

$$
E_{B}=\frac{539.3}{5}=107.86\,\mathrm{V/m}
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{B}=64.72\hat{a}_{y}-86.29\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{V/m}
$$

**Part 3(c) — Field at $P_{C}(5,6,1)$**

$P_{C}$ differs from $P_{B}$ only in $x$. Since the line is infinite and parallel to the $x$-axis, the geometry is identical:

$$
\mathbf{E}_{C}=\mathbf{E}_{B}=64.72\hat{a}_{y}-86.29\hat{a}_{z}\ \mathrm{V/m}
$$

questions.text: Find the electric field intensity in all three regions due to an infinite-sheet parallel-plate capacitor with surface charge densities $\rho_{S}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}$ and $-\rho_{S}\,\mathrm{C/m^{2}}$ placed at $y=0$ and $y=b$. Also, a uniform line charge of $3\,\mathrm{nC/m}$ lies at $y=3$ and a uniform surface charge $0.2\,\mathrm{nC/m^{2}}$ at $x=2$; find $\mathbf{E}$ at the origin.
questions.solution:
**Part 1, Step 1 — Field of a single infinite sheet**

For an infinite sheet of uniform charge density $\rho_{S}$, Gauss’s law gives

$$
\mathbf{E}=\frac{\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\,\hat{a}_{N}
$$

where $\hat{a}_{N}$ is the unit normal directed from the sheet toward the field point. The magnitude is independent of distance; only the direction changes as we cross the sheet.

**Part 1, Step 2 — Define the regions**

Sheet 1 at $y=0$ carries $+\rho_{S}$; Sheet 2 at $y=b$ carries $-\rho_{S}$ (with $b>0$):

| Region | Range | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $y<0$ | below both sheets |
| 2 | $0<y<b$ | between the sheets |
| 3 | $y>b$ | above both sheets |

**Part 1, Step 3 — Region 1 ($y<0$)**

Due to sheet 1 ($+\rho_{S}$ at $y=0$): field point below ⇒ $\hat{a}_{N}=-\hat{a}_{y}$:

$$
\mathbf{E}_{1}=\frac{\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(-\hat{a}_{y})
$$

Due to sheet 2 ($-\rho_{S}$ at $y=b$): density negative and point below ⇒ field along $+\hat{a}_{y}$:

$$
\mathbf{E}_{2}=\frac{-\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(-\hat{a}_{y})=\frac{\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(+\hat{a}_{y})
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{I}}=\mathbf{E}_{1}+\mathbf{E}_{2}=0
$$

**Part 1, Step 4 — Region 2 ($0<y<b$)**

Due to sheet 1: point above ⇒ $\hat{a}_{N}=+\hat{a}_{y}$:

$$
\mathbf{E}_{1}=\frac{\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(+\hat{a}_{y})
$$

Due to sheet 2: point below, negative density ⇒ field along $+\hat{a}_{y}$:

$$
\mathbf{E}_{2}=\frac{-\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(-\hat{a}_{y})=\frac{\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(+\hat{a}_{y})
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{II}}=\frac{\rho_{S}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\,\hat{a}_{y}
$$

**Part 1, Step 5 — Region 3 ($y>b$)**

Due to sheet 1: $\mathbf{E}_{1}=(\rho_{S}/(2\varepsilon_{0}))(+\hat{a}_{y})$.

Due to sheet 2: point above, negative density ⇒ field along $-\hat{a}_{y}$:

$$
\mathbf{E}_{2}=\frac{-\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(+\hat{a}_{y})=\frac{\rho_{S}}{2\varepsilon_{0}}(-\hat{a}_{y})
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{III}}=0
$$

**Part 1, Step 6 — Summary and physical meaning**

$$
\mathbf{E}=
\begin{cases}
0, & y<0\ \text{(Region 1)}\\[4pt]
