\mathbf{B}=\mu_{0}(\mathbf{H}+\mathbf{M}),\qquad\mathbf{M}=\chi_{m}\mathbf{H}.
$$

**Part 3 — Relative permeability**

$$
\mu_{r}=\frac{\mu}{\mu_{0}}=1+\chi_{m}\quad\text{(dimensionless)},
$$

how much more flux density a material produces than free space for the same $\mathbf{H}$. Classes: diamagnetic ($\mu_{r}<1$), paramagnetic ($\mu_{r}>1$ slightly), ferromagnetic ($\mu_{r}\gg 1$).

questions.text: Distinguish between conduction and displacement currents.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Definitions**

$$
\mathbf{J}_{c}=\sigma\mathbf{E},\qquad\mathbf{J}_{d}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}=\varepsilon\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}.
$$

**Step 2 — Distinction.** Conduction: real charge drift, needs a conductor, dissipates heat. Displacement: nothing moves — a changing $\mathbf{E}$ that produces $\mathbf{H}$ like a real current; exists in vacuum.

**Step 3 — Comparison.** See table in Question 6. Corrected Ampere:

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\sigma\mathbf{E}+\varepsilon\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t},\qquad
\frac{|\mathbf{J}_{c}|}{|\mathbf{J}_{d}|}=\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}=\tan\delta.
$$

**Step 4 — Capacitor.** In the leads $I_{c}$; between plates $I_{d}=d(DA)/dt=I_{c}$ exactly — continuity of current around the circuit.

questions.text: Derive the expression for Maxwell’s equation in point form.
questions.solution:
Each of Maxwell’s four equations is obtained from an experimental law in integral form, converted to point form by Stokes’s or the divergence theorem.

**Step 1 — Ampere (corrected)**

$$
\oint_{L}\mathbf{H}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=\int_{S}\left(\mathbf{J}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\right)\cdot d\mathbf{S}
\quad\xrightarrow{\text{Stokes}}\quad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}.
$$

**Step 2 — Faraday**

$$
\oint_{L}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=-\frac{d}{dt}\int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=-\int_{S}\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}\cdot d\mathbf{S}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}.
$$

**Step 3 — Gauss (electric)**

$$
\oint_{S}\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\int_{v}\rho_{v}\,dv
\quad\xrightarrow{\text{divergence}}\quad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}=\rho_{v}.
$$

**Step 4 — Gauss (magnetic)**

$$
\oint_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0.
$$

**Step 5 — Summary**

| Origin | Point form | Theorem |
|--------|------------|---------|
| Ampere (corrected) | $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t$ | Stokes |
| Faraday | $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\partial\mathbf{B}/\partial t$ | Stokes |
| Gauss (electric) | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}=\rho_{v}$ | Divergence |
| Gauss (magnetic) | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ | Divergence |

Completed by $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$, $J=\sigma E$.

questions.text: State and explain Maxwell’s equations in differential and integral form. Also define the displacement current and depth of penetration.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — The four equations**

| Law | Differential | Integral |
|-----|--------------|----------|
| Ampere | $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t$ | $\oint_{L}\mathbf{H}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=\int_{S}(\mathbf{J}+\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t)\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ |
| Faraday | $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\partial\mathbf{B}/\partial t$ | $\oint_{L}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=-d/dt\int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ |
| Gauss (E) | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}=\rho_{v}$ | $\oint_{S}\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}$ |
| Gauss (B) | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ | $\oint_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=0$ |

**Part 2 — Explanation.** (i) Changing $\mathbf{D}$ (and $\mathbf{J}$) produce circulating $\mathbf{H}$. (ii) Changing $\mathbf{B}$ produces circulating $\mathbf{E}$ (Lenz minus sign). (iii) Charge is a source of $\mathbf{D}$. (iv) No magnetic monopoles — $\mathbf{B}$ lines close. Together (i)+(ii) give waves at $u=1/\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}$.

**Part 3 — Auxiliary:** $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$, $J=\sigma E$, and continuity $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=-\partial\rho_{v}/\partial t$.

**Part 4 — Displacement current:** $\mathbf{J}_{d}=\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t$; required for charge conservation; $|\mathbf{J}_{c}|/|\mathbf{J}_{d}|=\sigma/(\omega\varepsilon)=\tan\delta$.

**Part 5 — Depth of penetration (skin depth).** For $E(z)=E_{0}e^{-\alpha z}$, $\delta=1/\alpha$ is the depth where amplitude falls to $1/e$. For a good conductor:

$$
\delta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}}.
$$

Copper at $60\,\mathrm{Hz}$: $\delta\approx 8.53\,\mathrm{mm}$; at $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$: $\delta\approx 66\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.
questions.answer: $\boxed{\text{Four Maxwell equations as tabulated};\ \mathbf{J}_{d}=\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t;\ \delta=1/\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}}$

questions.text: Write all the Maxwell equations for the time-varying field in point form as well as integral form.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Point and integral forms**

| # | Point form | Integral form | Name |
|---|------------|---------------|------|
| 1 | $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t$ | $\oint\mathbf{H}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=\int(\mathbf{J}+\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t)\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ | Ampere (corrected) |
| 2 | $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\partial\mathbf{B}/\partial t$ | $\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=-d/dt\int\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$ | Faraday |
| 3 | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}=\rho_{v}$ | $\oint\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}$ | Gauss (electric) |
| 4 | $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ | $\oint\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=0$ | Gauss (magnetic) |

**Step 2 — Constitutive:** $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$, $J=\sigma E$.

**Step 3 — Static vs.\ time-varying:** only the two curl equations change; setting $\partial/\partial t=0$ recovers static forms.

**Step 4 — Phasor:** $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)\mathbf{E}_{s}$, $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu\mathbf{H}_{s}$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}_{s}=\rho_{vs}$, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}_{s}=0$.
questions.answer: $\boxed{\text{Four equations in point \& integral form as in Step 1, plus }D=\varepsilon E,\ B=\mu H,\ J=\sigma E}$

questions.text: State Maxwell’s fourth equation.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Statement (Hayt ordering)**

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0\qquad\text{(point)},\qquad
\oint_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=0\qquad\text{(integral)}.
$$

**Step 2 — Meaning.** Net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero; $\mathbf{B}$ is solenoidal.

**Step 3 — Physical:** magnetic monopoles do not exist; $\mathbf{B}$ lines form closed loops; $B_{N1}=B_{N2}$ at interfaces. Permits $\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}$.

questions.text: How does Ampere’s law conflict with the continuity equation, and how is it corrected? Derive the conduction and displacement current in a capacitor.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Conflict and correction**

$\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}$ implies $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=0$, contradicting $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=-\partial\rho_{v}/\partial t$ unless currents are steady. Adding $\mathbf{J}_{d}$:

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}_{d}=\frac{\partial\rho_{v}}{\partial t}=\nabla\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathbf{J}_{d}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}.
$$

**Part 2 — Capacitor** with $V=V_{0}\sin\omega t$, $C=\varepsilon A/d$:

$$
I_{c}=\frac{dQ}{dt}=\omega C V_{0}\cos\omega t.
$$

Between plates $E=(V_{0}/d)\sin\omega t$, $D=\varepsilon E$,

$$
I_{d}=J_{d}A=\omega C V_{0}\cos\omega t=I_{c}.
$$

Displacement current in the gap equals conduction current in the leads — circuit continuity restored.
questions.answer: $\boxed{\text{Conflict: }\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=0\ \text{vs continuity};\ \mathbf{J}_{d}=\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t;\ I_{c}=I_{d}=\omega C V_{0}\cos\omega t}$

questions.text: How does $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}$ conflict with the continuity equation in time-varying fields? How is this conflict rectified in such fields?
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Conflict**

$$
\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})=\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=0,
$$

but continuity requires $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=-\partial\rho_{v}/\partial t$. Valid only for steady currents. Capacitor paradox: same Amperian path, two surfaces, two $I_{\mathrm{enc}}$.

**Part 2 — Rectification**

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\mathbf{J}_{d},\quad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}_{d}=\frac{\partial\rho_{v}}{\partial t}=\nabla\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathbf{J}_{d}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}.
$$

Corrected:

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t},
$$

whose divergence is the continuity equation. Predicted EM waves at $1/\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}$.

questions.text: Correct the equation $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=0$ for the time-varying field with necessary derivation. Also modify the equation $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\sigma\mathbf{E}$ with necessary arguments and derivation for the time-varying field.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Correcting $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=0$**

Static: $\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=0\Rightarrow\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=0$. Faraday requires $\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}\neq 0$. With stationary $L$, $S$:

$$
\oint_{L}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=-\int_{S}\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}\cdot d\mathbf{S}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}.
$$

**Part 2 — Modifying $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\sigma\mathbf{E}$**

$\nabla\cdot(\sigma\mathbf{E})=\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=0$ conflicts with continuity. Adding $\mathbf{J}_{d}=\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t$:

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\sigma\mathbf{E}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}=\sigma\mathbf{E}+\varepsilon\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t},
$$

with loss tangent $\sigma/(\omega\varepsilon)=\tan\delta$. Together with Faraday’s correction, the curl equations sustain electromagnetic waves.

questions.text: Derive the expressions for electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ for a uniform plane wave propagating in free space.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Maxwell’s equations in free space**

Free space: $\rho_{v}=0$, $\mathbf{J}=0$ ($\sigma=0$), $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{0}$, $\mu=\mu_{0}$:

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\mu_{0}\frac{\partial\mathbf{H}}{\partial t},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\varepsilon_{0}\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}=0,\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{H}=0.
$$

**Step 2 — Uncouple the equations**

Curl of Faraday’s law, then substitute Ampere’s law:

$$
\nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\mu_{0}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})
=-\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^{2}}.
$$

**Step 3 — Apply the vector identity**

$$
\nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E})-\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}=-\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}
$$

(since $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}=0$), so

$$
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}=\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^{2}},\qquad
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{H}=\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{H}}{\partial t^{2}}.
$$

**Step 4 — Identify the wave speed**

Compare with $\nabla^{2}\psi=(1/u^{2})\partial^{2}\psi/\partial t^{2}$:

$$
u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}}=c=3\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}.
$$

**Step 5 — Uniform plane wave along $+z$**

With $\partial/\partial x=\partial/\partial y=0$ and $\mathbf{E}=E_{x}(z,t)\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}$:

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}E_{x}}{\partial z^{2}}=\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}\frac{\partial^{2}E_{x}}{\partial t^{2}}.
$$

**Step 6 — Time-harmonic solution**

$$
\mathbf{E}=E_{0}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{V/m},\qquad
\beta=\omega\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}=\omega/c\ \mathrm{rad/m}.
$$

**Step 7 — Obtain $\mathbf{H}$ from Faraday’s law**

$$
\frac{\partial E_{x}}{\partial z}=E_{0}\beta\sin(\omega t-\beta z)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{\partial\mathbf{H}}{\partial t}=-\frac{E_{0}\beta}{\mu_{0}}\sin(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}.
$$

Integrating:

$$
\mathbf{H}=\frac{E_{0}\beta}{\mu_{0}\omega}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}.
$$

**Step 8 — Intrinsic impedance**

$$
\frac{\beta}{\mu_{0}\omega}=\frac{1}{\eta_{0}},\qquad
\eta_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{0}}{\varepsilon_{0}}}=120\pi\approx 377\,\Omega
$$

$$
\mathbf{H}=\frac{E_{0}}{\eta_{0}}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{A/m}.
$$

**Step 9 — Properties**

TEM ($\mathbf{E}\perp\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$, $\mathbf{H}\perp\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$); $\mathbf{E}\perp\mathbf{H}$; $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}\parallel\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$; in phase ($\eta_{0}$ real); $|\mathbf{E}|/|\mathbf{H}|=\eta_{0}$; no attenuation ($\alpha=0$).
questions.marksRaw: [8] 2080 Baishakh; 2078 Bhadra; 2068 Chaitra; 2069 Chaitra (E only); 2072 Chaitra; 2074 Ashwin (perfect dielectric)

questions.text: Derive the expression for electric and magnetic fields for a uniform plane wave propagating in a dissipative (lossy) medium.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Maxwell equations (lossy, phasor)**

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu\mathbf{H}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=0,\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{H}_{s}=0.
$$

**Step 2 — Helmholtz equation**

Curl of Faraday, substitute Ampere, use $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=0$:

$$
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}=\gamma^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\gamma^{2}=j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon),\qquad
\gamma=\alpha+j\beta.
$$

**Step 3 — Forward wave solution**

$$
E_{xs}=E_{0}e^{-\gamma z}=E_{0}e^{-\alpha z}e^{-j\beta z}
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}=E_{0}e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{V/m}.
$$

**Step 4 — Magnetic field**

$$
\mathbf{H}_{s}=\frac{E_{0}}{\eta}e^{-\gamma z}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y},\qquad
\eta=\sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon}}=|\eta|\angle\theta_{\eta}.
$$

**Step 5 — Time domain**

Because $\eta$ is complex, $\mathbf{H}$ lags $\mathbf{E}$ by $\theta_{\eta}$:

$$
\mathbf{H}=\frac{E_{0}}{|\eta|}e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\omega t-\beta z-\theta_{\eta})\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{A/m}.
$$

**Step 6 — Comparison**

| | Free space | Lossy medium |
|--|------------|--------------|
| $\gamma$ | $j\beta$ | $\alpha+j\beta$ |
| Amplitude | constant | decays as $e^{-\alpha z}$ |
| $\eta$ | $377\,\Omega$ real | $\|\eta\|\angle\theta_{\eta}$ |
| $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{H}$ | in phase | $\mathbf{H}$ lags by $\theta_{\eta}$ |
questions.answer:
$\boxed{\mathbf{E}=E_{0}e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x};\ \mathbf{H}=(E_{0}/|\eta|)e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\omega t-\beta z-\theta_{\eta})\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y};\ \gamma=\sqrt{j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)},\ \eta=\sqrt{j\omega\mu/(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)}}$

---

questions.text: List out the Maxwell equations in phasor form for the time-varying case in free space. Derive the wave equation for a wave propagating in a lossy medium.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Phasor Maxwell equations (free space)**

With $\partial/\partial t\to j\omega$, $\rho_{v}=0$, $\mathbf{J}=0$:

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu_{0}\mathbf{H}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=j\omega\varepsilon_{0}\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=0,\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{H}_{s}=0.
$$

**Part 2 — Wave equation in a lossy medium**

With finite $\sigma$:

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu\mathbf{H}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=0.
$$

($\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=0$ holds in the steady time-harmonic state because free charge decays as $e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau=\varepsilon/\sigma$.)

Curl of Faraday, substitute Ampere, apply $\nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}$:

$$
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}-\gamma^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}=0,\qquad
\gamma^{2}=j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon),
$$

and likewise $\nabla^{2}\mathbf{H}_{s}-\gamma^{2}\mathbf{H}_{s}=0$. Forward solution: $E_{xs}=E_{0}e^{-\gamma z}=E_{0}e^{-\alpha z}e^{-j\beta z}$.

Special cases: lossless $\sigma=0\Rightarrow\gamma=j\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$; good conductor $\sigma\gg\omega\varepsilon\Rightarrow\alpha=\beta=\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}$.

questions.text: List out the point form of Maxwell’s equations in phasor form for the time-varying case. Using these equations, derive the electric field component of a uniform plane wave travelling in a perfect dielectric medium.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — General phasor Maxwell equations**

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu\mathbf{H}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}_{s}=\rho_{vs},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}_{s}=0.
$$

**Part 2 — Perfect dielectric** ($\sigma=0$, $\rho_{v}=0$, $\varepsilon,\mu$ real)

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu\mathbf{H}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=j\omega\varepsilon\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=0.
$$

Curl elimination yields

$$
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}+\omega^{2}\mu\varepsilon\mathbf{E}_{s}=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\gamma=j\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon},\quad\alpha=0,\quad\beta=\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}.
$$

For $+z$ travel, $E_{x}$-polarised: $E_{xs}=E_{0}e^{-j\beta z}$, so

$$
\mathbf{E}=E_{0}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{V/m},
$$

with

$$
u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}},\qquad
\eta=\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}}\ \text{(real)},\qquad
\mathbf{H}=\frac{E_{0}}{\eta}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}.
$$

questions.text: Establish the relation for Helmholtz’s equation for electromagnetic wave propagation.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Start from phasor Maxwell curl equations**

$$
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu\mathbf{H}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=0,\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{H}_{s}=0.
$$

**Step 2 — Eliminate $\mathbf{H}_{s}$**

$$
\nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)\mathbf{E}_{s}.
$$

**Step 3 — Vector identity**

$$
\nabla\times\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=\nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s})-\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}=-\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}.
$$

**Step 4 — Helmholtz equation**

$$
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}-\gamma^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}=0,\qquad
\gamma^{2}=j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon),
$$

and similarly $\nabla^{2}\mathbf{H}_{s}-\gamma^{2}\mathbf{H}_{s}=0$.

| Medium | $\gamma^{2}$ | $\gamma$ |
|--------|--------------|----------|
| Free space / lossless | $-\omega^{2}\mu\varepsilon$ | $j\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$ ($\alpha=0$) |
| Good conductor | $\approx j\omega\mu\sigma$ | $(1+j)\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}$ |
| General lossy | $j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)$ | $\alpha+j\beta$ |

questions.text: Consider a wave propagating in a lossy dielectric with propagation constant $\gamma=\alpha+j\beta$. Derive expressions for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ if the medium is characterized by permittivity $\varepsilon$, permeability $\mu$ and conductivity $\sigma$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Expand $\gamma^{2}$**

$$
\gamma^{2}=j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)=-\omega^{2}\mu\varepsilon+j\omega\mu\sigma.
$$

**Step 2 — Expand $(\alpha+j\beta)^{2}$**

$$
\gamma^{2}=(\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2})+j(2\alpha\beta).
$$

**Step 3 — Equate parts**

$$
\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2}=-\omega^{2}\mu\varepsilon,\qquad 2\alpha\beta=\omega\mu\sigma.
$$

**Step 4 — Equate magnitudes**

$$
\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}=\omega\mu\sqrt{\sigma^{2}+\omega^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}.
$$

**Step 5 — Solve**

$$
\alpha=\omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\varepsilon}{2}\left(\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^{2}}-1\right)}\ \mathrm{Np/m}
$$

$$
\beta=\omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\varepsilon}{2}\left(\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^{2}}+1\right)}\ \mathrm{rad/m}
$$

**Checks:** $\sigma=0\Rightarrow\alpha=0$, $\beta=\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$; $\sigma\gg\omega\varepsilon\Rightarrow\alpha=\beta=\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}$.

questions.text: Define the Poynting vector. Using this, deduce the time-average power density for a dissipative medium.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Definition**

$$
\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}\ \mathrm{W/m}^{2}
$$

— instantaneous power density; direction = power flow. Total power: $\displaystyle\oint_{S}\mathbf{P}\cdot d\mathbf{S}$.

**Part 2 — Fields in a dissipative medium**

$$
\mathbf{E}=E_{0}e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x},
$$

$$
\mathbf{H}=\frac{E_{0}}{|\eta|}e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\omega t-\beta z-\theta_{\eta})\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}.
$$

**Part 3 — Instantaneous Poynting vector**

$$
\mathbf{P}=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{|\eta|}e^{-2\alpha z}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\cos(\omega t-\beta z-\theta_{\eta})\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}.
$$

Using $\cos A\cos B=\tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)]$ and averaging over a period (double-frequency term vanishes):

$$
\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2|\eta|}e^{-2\alpha z}\cos\theta_{\eta}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{W/m}^{2}.
$$

Phasor check: $\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{Re}\{\mathbf{E}_{s}\times\mathbf{H}_{s}^{*}\}$ gives the same result. Lossless limit ($\alpha=0$, $\theta_{\eta}=0$): $E_{0}^{2}/(2\eta)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$.

questions.text: State and prove Poynting’s theorem.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Statement**

$$
\oint_{S}(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H})\cdot d\mathbf{S}
=-\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{v}\left(\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon E^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mu H^{2}\right)\,dv
-\int_{v}\sigma E^{2}\,dv.
$$

**Step 2 — Proof outline**

From $\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\partial\mathbf{D}/\partial t$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\partial\mathbf{B}/\partial t$, form $\mathbf{E}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})$ and use

$$
\nabla\cdot(\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H})=\mathbf{H}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{E})-\mathbf{E}\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{H}).
$$

Recognise

$$
\mathbf{E}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon E^{2}\right),\quad
\mathbf{H}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\!\left(\frac{1}{2}\mu H^{2}\right),\quad
\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{J}=\sigma E^{2}.
$$

Integrate and apply the divergence theorem to obtain the integral form above.

questions.text:
State Poynting’s theorem. An EM wave travels in free space with the electric field component
$\mathbf{E}=(10\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}+5\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z})\cos(\omega t+2y-4z)\ \mathrm{V/m}$.
Find (a) $\omega$ and $\lambda$; (b) the magnetic field component; (c) the time-average power in the wave.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Statement:** as in Question 2.

**Part (a)** — Phase $\omega t+2y-4z$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mathbf{k}=-2\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}+4\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$:

$$
\beta=|\mathbf{k}|=\sqrt{20}=4.472\,\mathrm{rad/m},\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}=-0.4472\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}+0.8944\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}.
$$

$$
\omega=\beta c=1.342\times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{rad/s},\qquad
\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}=1.405\,\mathrm{m}.
$$

**Part (b)** — $\mathbf{H}=(1/\eta_{0})\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}\times\mathbf{E}$:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}\times\mathbf{E}_{0}=-11.18\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathbf{H}=-29.66\cos(\omega t+2y-4z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{mA/m}.
$$

**Part (c)**

$$
\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{|\mathbf{E}_{0}|^{2}}{2\eta_{0}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}
=-0.0741\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}+0.1483\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{W/m}^{2},
\quad
|\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{avg}}|=165.8\,\mathrm{mW/m}^{2}.
$$

questions.text: Explain the term skin depth. Using the Poynting vector, deduce the time-average power density for a perfect dielectric.
questions.solution:
**Part 1 — Skin depth**

In a conductor $E(z)=E_{0}e^{-\alpha z}$. Skin depth $\delta$ is the distance at which the amplitude falls to $1/e$ (36.8%) of the surface value:

$$
\delta=\frac{1}{\alpha}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}}\ \text{(good conductor)}.
$$

**Part 2 — Perfect dielectric** ($\sigma=0$, $\alpha=0$, $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$ real)

$$
\mathbf{P}=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{\eta}\cos^{2}(\omega t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{E_{0}^{2}}{2\eta}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{W/m}^{2}.
$$

questions.text: Determine the skin depth, propagation constant and velocity of a wave at $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ in a good conductor with conductivity $1.9\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{mho/m}$.
questions.solution:
$f=10^{6}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $\sigma=1.9\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{S/m}$, $\mu=\mu_{0}$:

$$
\alpha=\beta=\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}=8660.8\,\mathrm{Np/m\ (rad/m)}
$$

$$
\delta=\frac{1}{\alpha}=0.1155\,\mathrm{mm}=115.5\,\mu\mathrm{m}
$$

$$
\gamma=8660.8+j8660.8\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}=12248\angle 45^{\circ}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}
$$

$$
u=\frac{\omega}{\beta}=\frac{2\pi\times 10^{6}}{8660.8}=725.5\,\mathrm{m/s}.
$$

questions.text: Write short notes on: (a) Loss tangent; (b) Skin depth.
questions.solution:
**(a) Loss tangent**

$$
\tan\delta=\frac{|J_{c}|}{|J_{d}|}=\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}.
$$

$\ll 1$: good dielectric; $\gg 1$: good conductor. Classification depends on frequency, not material alone.

**(b) Skin depth**

$$
\delta=\frac{1}{\alpha}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}}
$$

— depth at which the field falls to $36.8\%$ of its surface value; cause of the skin effect. Valid when $\tan\delta\gg 1$.

questions.text: For a non-magnetic material having $\varepsilon_{r}=2.25$ and $\sigma=10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mho/m}$, find at $5\,\mathrm{MHz}$: (a) loss tangent; (b) attenuation constant; (c) phase constant; (d) intrinsic impedance.
questions.solution:
$\mu=\mu_{0}$, $\varepsilon=2.25\varepsilon_{0}$, $\omega=2\pi\times 5\times 10^{6}=3.1416\times 10^{7}$:

**(a)** $\tan\delta=\sigma/(\omega\varepsilon)=0.16$.

**(b)–(c)** Exact formulas:

$$
\alpha=0.01252\,\mathrm{Np/m},\qquad \beta=0.1577\,\mathrm{rad/m}.
$$

**(d)** $\eta=j\omega\mu/(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)=249.6\angle 4.54^{\circ}\,\Omega=248.8+j19.8\,\Omega$.

questions.text: A uniform plane wave in free space is propagating in the $-\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}$ direction at a frequency of $5\,\mathrm{MHz}$. If $\mathbf{E}=200\cos(\omega t+\beta y)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{V/m}$, write the expressions for $\mathbf{E}_{s}$ and $\mathbf{H}_{s}$ in phasor form.
questions.solution:
$$
\omega=2\pi\times 5\times 10^{6},\qquad
\beta=\omega/c=0.1047\,\mathrm{rad/m}.
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{s}=200e^{j0.1047y}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{V/m}.
$$

With $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}=-\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}$:

$$
\mathbf{H}_{s}=\frac{1}{\eta_{0}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-0.5305e^{j0.1047y}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{A/m}.
$$

questions.text: A uniform plane wave in free space is given by $\mathbf{H}_{s}=250\angle 30^{\circ}\,e^{-j350z}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{A/m}$ (units corrected from printed V/m). Determine the phase constant, frequency, intrinsic impedance, $\mathbf{E}_{s}$, and $|\mathbf{H}|$ at $z=25\,\mathrm{mm}$, $t=4\,\mathrm{ps}$.
questions.solution:
$$
\beta=350\,\mathrm{rad/m},\qquad
f=\beta c/(2\pi)=16.71\,\mathrm{GHz},\qquad
\eta=\eta_{0}=377\,\Omega.
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{s}=\eta_{0}\mathbf{H}_{s}\times\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}=-94250\angle 30^{\circ}\,e^{-j350z}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{V/m}.
$$

At the given point: $|\mathbf{H}|=11.90\,\mathrm{A/m}$.

questions.text: A uniform plane wave in free space is given by $\mathbf{H}_{s}=400\angle 30^{\circ}e^{-j250z}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{A/m}$. Find: (a) $\omega$; (b) $\lambda$ and $\eta$; (c) $\mathbf{E}(x,y,z,t)$ at $z=50\,\mathrm{mm}$, $t=4\,\mathrm{ps}$.
questions.solution:
**(a)** $\beta=250\Rightarrow\omega=\beta c=7.5\times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

**(b)** $\lambda=2\pi/\beta=25.13\,\mathrm{mm}$, $\eta=377\,\Omega$.

**(c)** $\mathbf{E}_{s}=150800\angle 30^{\circ}e^{-j250z}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}$, so

$$
\mathbf{E}=150800\cos(7.5\times 10^{10}t-250z+30^{\circ})\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{V/m};
$$

at the given point $\mathbf{E}=94.9\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{kV/m}$.

questions.text: A $1\,\mathrm{MHz}$ uniform plane wave with amplitude $25\,\mathrm{V/m}$ propagates along $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}$ in a material with $\varepsilon_{r}=4$, $\mu_{r}=9$, $\sigma=0$. Find: (a) velocity; (b) phase constant; (c) intrinsic impedance; (d) $\mathbf{E}(t)$ if $E_{z}=0$ and $E_{y}=25\,\mathrm{V/m}$ at $P(10,10,10)$ at $100\,\mathrm{ns}$; (e) $\mathbf{H}(t)$.
questions.solution:
**(a)** $u=c/\sqrt{\mu_{r}\varepsilon_{r}}=c/6=5\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

**(b)** $\beta=\omega/u=0.1257\,\mathrm{rad/m}$.

**(c)** $\eta=\eta_{0}\sqrt{\mu_{r}/\varepsilon_{r}}=377\times 1.5=565.5\,\Omega$.

**(d)** Phase condition gives $\phi=36^{\circ}$:

$$
\mathbf{E}=25\cos(6.2832\times 10^{6}t-0.1257x+36^{\circ})\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{V/m}.
$$

**(e)**

$$
\mathbf{H}=44.21\cos(6.2832\times 10^{6}t-0.1257x+36^{\circ})\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{mA/m}.
$$

questions.text: A $9.375\,\mathrm{GHz}$ uniform plane wave propagates in polythene ($\varepsilon_{r}=2.26$, $\mu_{r}=1$). If the material is lossless, find the phase constant, wavelength, velocity of propagation and intrinsic impedance.
questions.solution:
$$
u=\frac{c}{\sqrt{2.26}}=1.996\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s},\qquad
\beta=\frac{\omega}{u}=295.2\,\mathrm{rad/m},
$$

$$
\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}=21.29\,\mathrm{mm},\qquad
\eta=\frac{\eta_{0}}{\sqrt{2.26}}=250.8\,\Omega.
$$

questions.text: A $9.4\,\mathrm{GHz}$ uniform plane wave propagates in a medium with $\varepsilon_{r}=2.25$, $\mu_{r}=1$. If $|\mathbf{H}|=7\,\mathrm{mA/m}$ and the material is lossless, find: (i) $u$; (ii) $\lambda$; (iii) $\beta$; (iv) $\eta$; (v) $|\mathbf{E}|$.
questions.solution:
$$
u=\frac{c}{1.5}=2\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s},\quad
\lambda=\frac{u}{f}=21.28\,\mathrm{mm},\quad
\beta=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}=295.3\,\mathrm{rad/m},
$$

$$
\eta=\frac{377}{1.5}=251.3\,\Omega,\quad
|\mathbf{E}|=\eta|\mathbf{H}|=1.759\,\mathrm{V/m}.
$$

questions.text: A uniform plane wave has $\mathbf{H}=15\cos(2\times 10^{8}t+\beta x)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{A/m}$ in a medium with $\sigma=0$, $\varepsilon=4\varepsilon_{0}$, $\mu=\mu_{0}$. Find: (a) direction of propagation, $\beta$, $\lambda$, $v_{p}$, $\eta$; (b) $|\mathbf{H}|$; (c) $\mathbf{E}$.
questions.solution:
Phase $+\beta x\Rightarrow\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}=-\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}$.

$$
v_{p}=\frac{c}{2}=1.5\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s},\quad
\beta=\frac{\omega}{v_{p}}=1.333\,\mathrm{rad/m},\quad
\lambda=4.712\,\mathrm{m},\quad
\eta=\frac{377}{2}=188.5\,\Omega.
$$

$$
|\mathbf{H}|=15\,\mathrm{A/m},\qquad
\mathbf{E}=2827.5\cos(2\times 10^{8}t+1.333x)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{V/m}.
$$

questions.text: Given $\mathbf{E}(z,t)=1800\cos(10^{7}\pi t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $\mathbf{H}(z,t)=3.8\cos(10^{7}\pi t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{A/m}$ propagating at $u=1.4\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in a perfect dielectric, find: (a) $\beta$; (b) $\lambda$; (c) $\eta$; (d) $\mu_{r}$; (e) $\varepsilon_{r}$.
questions.solution:
$$
\omega=10^{7}\pi,\quad
\beta=\omega/u=0.2244\,\mathrm{rad/m},\quad
\lambda=28.0\,\mathrm{m},\quad
\eta=E_{0}/H_{0}=473.7\,\Omega.
$$

From $\sqrt{\mu_{r}\varepsilon_{r}}=c/u=2.1429$ and $\sqrt{\mu_{r}/\varepsilon_{r}}=\eta/\eta_{0}=1.2565$:

$$
\mu_{r}=2.69,\qquad\varepsilon_{r}=1.71.
$$

questions.text: A uniform plane wave in a non-magnetic medium has $\mathbf{E}=50\cos(10^{8}t+2z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{V/m}$. Find: (i) direction of propagation; (ii) $\beta$, $\lambda$, $v_{p}$, $\varepsilon_{r}$, $\eta$; (iii) $\mathbf{H}$.
questions.solution:
**(i)** $+\beta z\Rightarrow\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}=-\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$.

**(ii)** $\beta=2\,\mathrm{rad/m}$, $\lambda=3.142\,\mathrm{m}$, $v_{p}=\omega/\beta=5\times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\varepsilon_{r}=(c/v_{p})^{2}=36$, $\eta=\eta_{0}/\sqrt{\varepsilon_{r}}=62.83\,\Omega$.

**(iii)** $\mathbf{H}=795.8\cos(10^{8}t+2z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{mA/m}$.

questions.text:
A lossless dielectric has $\sigma=0$, $\mu_{r}=1$, $\varepsilon_{r}=4$. An EM wave has
$\mathbf{H}=-0.1\cos(\omega t-z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}+0.5\sin(\omega t-z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{A/m}$.
Find: (a) $\omega$; (b) $\eta$; (c) $\mathbf{E}$.
questions.solution:
$\beta=1\,\mathrm{rad/m}$, $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{k}=+\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$.

**(a)** $v_{p}=c/2=1.5\times 10^{8}\Rightarrow\omega=\beta v_{p}=1.5\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

**(b)** $\eta=\eta_{0}/2=188.5\,\Omega$.

**(c)** $\mathbf{E}=\eta\mathbf{H}\times\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}$:

$$
\mathbf{E}=94.25\sin(1.5\times 10^{8}t-z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}+18.85\cos(1.5\times 10^{8}t-z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{V/m}.
$$

questions.text: A uniform plane wave in free space is given by $\mathbf{E}=2\cos(10^{7}\pi t-\beta z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}$; determine $\beta$ and $\mathbf{H}$.
questions.solution:
$$
\omega=10^{7}\pi\Rightarrow f=5\,\mathrm{MHz},\qquad
\beta=\omega/c=0.1047\,\mathrm{rad/m}.
$$

$$
\mathbf{H}=\frac{1}{\eta_{0}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\times\mathbf{E}=5.305\cos(10^{7}\pi t-0.1047z)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{mA/m}.
$$

questions.text: The phasor electric field in free space is $\mathbf{E}_{s}=100\angle 45^{\circ}\,e^{-j50z}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x}\ \mathrm{V/m}$. Determine the frequency, wave impedance, $\mathbf{H}_{s}$, and $|\mathbf{E}|$ at $z=10\,\mathrm{mm}$, $t=20\,\mathrm{ps}$.
questions.solution:
$$
\beta=50\,\mathrm{rad/m}\Rightarrow f=\beta c/(2\pi)=2.387\,\mathrm{GHz},\qquad\eta=377\,\Omega.
$$

$$
\mathbf{H}_{s}=265.3\angle 45^{\circ}\,e^{-j50z}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{mA/m}.
$$

At the given point: $|\mathbf{E}|=83.35\,\mathrm{V/m}$.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the Standing Wave Ratio (SWR), indicating where on the $z$-axis you will get the maximum and minimum value of $E$. Assume the boundary is at $z=0$, region $z<0$ is a perfect dielectric, and region $z>0$ may be of any material.
questions.solution:
In region 1 ($z<0$): incident $E_{is}=E_{i0}e^{-j\beta_{1}z}$, reflected $E_{rs}=\Gamma E_{i0}e^{j\beta_{1}z}$ with $\Gamma=|\Gamma|e^{j\phi}$.

$$
|E_{1s}|=|E_{i0}|\,\bigl|1+|\Gamma|e^{j\theta}\bigr|,\qquad\theta=\phi+2\beta_{1}z.
$$

$$
|E|_{\max}=|E_{i0}|(1+|\Gamma|),\qquad
|E|_{\min}=|E_{i0}|(1-|\Gamma|),
$$

$$
s=\frac{|E|_{\max}}{|E|_{\min}}=\frac{1+|\Gamma|}{1-|\Gamma|},\qquad
|\Gamma|=\frac{s-1}{s+1}.
$$

$$
z_{\max}=\frac{-2n\pi+\phi}{2\beta_{1}},\qquad
z_{\min}=\frac{-(2n+1)\pi+\phi}{2\beta_{1}}.
$$

Spacing: $\lambda_{1}/2$ between like extrema; $\lambda_{1}/4$ between a max and the next min.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the standing wave for both electric and magnetic fields. Also indicate where on the $z$-axis you get max/min of $E$. Boundary at $z=0$; $z<0$ perfect dielectric; $z>0$ arbitrary.
questions.solution:
$$
\mathbf{E}_{1s}=E_{i0}\bigl(e^{-j\beta_{1}z}+\Gamma e^{j\beta_{1}z}\bigr)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x},
$$

$$
\mathbf{H}_{1s}=\frac{E_{i0}}{\eta_{1}}\bigl(e^{-j\beta_{1}z}-\Gamma e^{j\beta_{1}z}\bigr)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}.
$$

Maxima/minima of $E$ as in Question 1; $\mathbf{H}$ is maximum where $\mathbf{E}$ is minimum.

For a perfect conductor ($\Gamma=-1$):

$$
\mathbf{E}_{1}=2E_{i0}\sin(\beta_{1}z)\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{x},\qquad
\mathbf{H}_{1}=\frac{2E_{i0}}{\eta_{1}}\cos(\beta_{1}z)\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}
$$

— a pure standing wave with zero average power.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the input intrinsic impedance using the concept of reflection of uniform plane waves.
questions.solution:
For a slab (region 2, thickness $d$) between media 1 and 3, with $\Gamma_{d}=(\eta_{3}-\eta_{2})/(\eta_{3}+\eta_{2})$ at $z=d$:

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta_{2}\frac{1+\Gamma_{d}e^{-j2\beta_{2}d}}{1-\Gamma_{d}e^{-j2\beta_{2}d}}
=\eta_{2}\frac{\eta_{3}\cos\beta_{2}d+j\eta_{2}\sin\beta_{2}d}{\eta_{2}\cos\beta_{2}d+j\eta_{3}\sin\beta_{2}d}.
$$

Special cases: half-wave $d=\lambda_{2}/2\Rightarrow\eta_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta_{3}$; quarter-wave $d=\lambda_{2}/4\Rightarrow\eta_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta_{2}^{2}/\eta_{3}$.

questions.text: Explain the phenomenon when a plane wave is incident normally on the interface between two different media. Derive the expressions for reflection and transmission coefficient.
questions.solution:
At normal incidence the incident wave splits into reflected and transmitted parts to satisfy boundary conditions. Continuity of tangential $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ at $z=0$ yields

$$
\Gamma=\frac{E_{r0}}{E_{i0}}=\frac{\eta_{2}-\eta_{1}}{\eta_{2}+\eta_{1}},\qquad
\tau=\frac{E_{t0}}{E_{i0}}=\frac{2\eta_{2}}{\eta_{2}+\eta_{1}},\qquad
1+\Gamma=\tau.
$$

questions.text: A $z$-polarized uniform plane wave at $100\,\mathrm{MHz}$ propagates in air in the $+x$ direction and impinges normally on a perfectly conducting plane at $x=0$. With $E_{i0}=3\,\mathrm{mV/m}$, determine phasor and instantaneous expressions for: (a) incident $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{H}$; (b) reflected $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{H}$.
questions.solution:
$\beta=\omega/c=2.094\,\mathrm{rad/m}$, $\eta_{1}=377\,\Omega$, $\Gamma=-1$.

**(a)**

$$
\mathbf{E}_{is}=3\times 10^{-3}e^{-j2.094x}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{V/m},
\quad
\mathbf{H}_{is}=-7.958\times 10^{-6}e^{-j2.094x}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mathrm{A/m},
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{i}=3\cos(6.283\times 10^{8}t-2.094x)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{mV/m},
\quad
\mathbf{H}_{i}=-7.958\cos(6.283\times 10^{8}t-2.094x)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mu\mathrm{A/m}.
$$

**(b)**

$$
\mathbf{E}_{rs}=-3\times 10^{-3}e^{j2.094x}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z},\quad
\mathbf{H}_{rs}=-7.958\times 10^{-6}e^{j2.094x}\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y},
$$

$$
\mathbf{E}_{r}=-3\cos(6.283\times 10^{8}t+2.094x)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{z}\ \mathrm{mV/m},
\quad
\mathbf{H}_{r}=-7.958\cos(6.283\times 10^{8}t+2.094x)\,\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{y}\ \mu\mathrm{A/m}.
$$

questions.text: A uniform plane wave in air partially reflects from an unknown material. Measurements: $1.5\,\mathrm{m}$ between maxima; first maximum $0.75\,\mathrm{m}$ from the interface; SWR $=5$. Determine the intrinsic impedance of the unknown material.
questions.solution:
$\lambda/2=1.5\Rightarrow\lambda=3\,\mathrm{m}$. $|\Gamma|=(s-1)/(s+1)=0.6667$. First max at $z=-0.75=\lambda/4$ from interface $\Rightarrow$ minimum at interface $\Rightarrow\Gamma$ real and negative: $\Gamma=-0.6667$.

$$
\Gamma=\frac{\eta_{2}-377}{\eta_{2}+377}=-0.6667
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\eta_{2}=75.4\,\Omega.
$$

Check: $\eta_{2}=\eta_{1}/s=377/5=75.4\,\Omega$.

questions.text: A radar dish antenna needs to be covered with transparent plastic ($\varepsilon_{r}=2.25$, $\mu_{r}=1$) with no reflection back to the antenna. What should be the minimum thickness if the operating frequency is $10\,\mathrm{GHz}$?
questions.solution:
Air–plastic–air: need $\eta_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta_{0}$. With $\eta_{1}=\eta_{3}$, this requires $\sin\beta_{2}d=0\Rightarrow d=n\lambda_{2}/2$. Minimum ($n=1$):

$$
\lambda_{0}=\frac{c}{f}=3\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad
\lambda_{2}=\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{r}}}=2\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad
d_{\min}=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{2}=1\,\mathrm{cm}.
$$

questions.text: The parameters of a certain transmission line operating at $6\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ are $L=0.4\,\mu\mathrm{H/m}$, $C=40\,\mathrm{pF/m}$, $G=80\,\mathrm{mS/m}$ and $R=20\,\Omega/\mathrm{m}$. Find $\gamma$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\lambda$ and $Z_{0}$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Form the series impedance $R+j\omega L$**

$$
\omega=6\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{rad/s}
$$

$$
\omega L=(6\times 10^{8})(0.4\times 10^{-6})=240
$$

$$
R+j\omega L=20+j240
$$

In polar form:

$$
|R+j\omega L|=\sqrt{20^{2}+240^{2}}=\sqrt{400+57600}=\sqrt{58000}=240.83
$$

$$
\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{240}{20}\right)=\tan^{-1}(12)=85.24^{\circ}
$$

$$
R+j\omega L=240.83\angle 85.24^{\circ}\,\Omega/\mathrm{m}
$$

**Step 2 — Form the shunt admittance $G+j\omega C$**

$$
\omega C=(6\times 10^{8})(40\times 10^{-12})=0.024
$$

$$
G+j\omega C=0.08+j0.024
$$

$$
|G+j\omega C|=\sqrt{(0.08)^{2}+(0.024)^{2}}=\sqrt{0.0064+0.000576}=\sqrt{0.006976}=0.08352
$$

$$
\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{0.024}{0.08}\right)=\tan^{-1}(0.3)=16.70^{\circ}
$$

$$
G+j\omega C=0.08352\angle 16.70^{\circ}\,\mathrm{S/m}
$$

**Step 3 — Propagation constant**

For a product under a square root, multiply the magnitudes and add the angles, then halve the angle and root the magnitude:

$$
\gamma=\sqrt{(R+j\omega L)(G+j\omega C)}=\sqrt{(240.83\angle 85.24^{\circ})(0.08352\angle 16.70^{\circ})}=\sqrt{20.114\angle 101.94^{\circ}}
$$

$$
\gamma=\sqrt{20.114}\,\angle\frac{101.94^{\circ}}{2}=4.485\angle 50.97^{\circ}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}
$$

**Step 4 — Extract $\alpha$ and $\beta$**

Convert to rectangular form, since $\gamma=\alpha+j\beta$:

$$
\alpha=4.485\cos 50.97^{\circ}=4.485(0.6298)=2.824\,\mathrm{Np/m}
$$

$$
\beta=4.485\sin 50.97^{\circ}=4.485(0.7768)=3.484\,\mathrm{rad/m}
$$

$$
\gamma=2.824+j3.484\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}
$$

**Step 5 — Wavelength**

$$
\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}=\frac{6.2832}{3.484}=1.803\,\mathrm{m}
$$

**Step 6 — Characteristic impedance**

For a quotient under a square root, divide the magnitudes and subtract the angles:

$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{R+j\omega L}{G+j\omega C}}=\sqrt{\frac{240.83\angle 85.24^{\circ}}{0.08352\angle 16.70^{\circ}}}=\sqrt{2883.4\angle 68.54^{\circ}}
$$

$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{2883.4}\,\angle\frac{68.54^{\circ}}{2}=53.70\angle 34.27^{\circ}\,\Omega=44.4+j30.2\,\Omega
$$

**Step 7 — Comment**

Note how lossy this line is. Compare the two loss ratios:

$$
\frac{R}{\omega L}=\frac{20}{240}=0.083\qquad\text{(series losses modest)}
$$

$$
\frac{G}{\omega C}=\frac{0.08}{0.024}=3.33\qquad\text{(shunt losses dominate)}
$$

The shunt conductance is the main culprit, and because the two ratios are unequal, the line is not distortionless — $Z_{0}$ comes out complex ($\angle 34.27^{\circ}$), and both $\alpha$ and $u$ vary with frequency. Also

$$
u=\frac{\omega}{\beta}=\frac{6\times 10^{8}}{3.484}=1.72\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}
$$

questions.text: A transmission line operating at $120\,\mathrm{MHz}$ has $R=20\,\Omega/\mathrm{m}$, $L=0.3\,\mu\mathrm{H/m}$, $C=63\,\mathrm{pF/m}$ and $G=4.2\,\mathrm{mS/m}$. Find: (a) the propagation coefficient $\gamma$; (b) the velocity of wave propagation on the line $v$; (c) the characteristic impedance $Z_{0}$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Look before leaping: test for the distortionless condition**

Before grinding through complex arithmetic, check whether this line satisfies $R/L=G/C$:

$$
\frac{R}{L}=\frac{20}{0.3\times 10^{-6}}=6.667\times 10^{7}
$$

$$
\frac{G}{C}=\frac{4.2\times 10^{-3}}{63\times 10^{-12}}=6.667\times 10^{7}
$$

$$
\frac{R}{L}=\frac{G}{C}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{this is a distortionless line}
$$

The numbers were chosen deliberately. This turns a messy problem into a clean one — but the general formulas would of course give the same answers, and Step 5 confirms it.

**Step 2 — Collect the constants**

$$
f=120\,\mathrm{MHz},\qquad \omega=2\pi\times 120\times 10^{6}=7.540\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{rad/s}
$$

$$
\sqrt{LC}=\sqrt{(0.3\times 10^{-6})(63\times 10^{-12})}=\sqrt{1.89\times 10^{-17}}=4.347\times 10^{-9}
$$

**Step 3 — Part (a): Propagation coefficient**

For a distortionless line the general expression collapses. Writing $k=R/L=G/C$:

$$
R+j\omega L=L(k+j\omega),\qquad G+j\omega C=C(k+j\omega)
$$

$$
\gamma=\sqrt{LC}\,(k+j\omega)=k\sqrt{LC}+j\omega\sqrt{LC}
$$

$$
\alpha=k\sqrt{LC}=\sqrt{RG}=\sqrt{(20)(4.2\times 10^{-3})}=\sqrt{0.084}=0.2898\,\mathrm{Np/m}
$$

$$
\beta=\omega\sqrt{LC}=(7.540\times 10^{8})(4.347\times 10^{-9})=3.278\,\mathrm{rad/m}
$$

$$
\gamma=0.2898+j3.278\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}=3.291\angle 84.95^{\circ}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}
$$

**Step 4 — Part (b): Velocity of propagation**

$$
v=\frac{\omega}{\beta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}=\frac{1}{4.347\times 10^{-9}}=2.300\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}
$$

Check: $v=\omega/\beta=(7.540\times 10^{8})/3.278=2.300\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ ✓ (about $0.77c$, typical for a real cable).

**Step 5 — Part (c): Characteristic impedance**

For a distortionless line the $(k+j\omega)$ factors cancel in the quotient:

$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{L(k+j\omega)}{C(k+j\omega)}}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.3\times 10^{-6}}{63\times 10^{-12}}}=\sqrt{4762}=69.0\,\Omega\quad\text{(purely real)}
$$

**Step 6 — Verification via the general formulas**

$$
\omega L=(7.540\times 10^{8})(0.3\times 10^{-6})=226.2\quad\Rightarrow\quad R+j\omega L=20+j226.2=227.1\angle 84.95^{\circ}
$$

$$
\omega C=(7.540\times 10^{8})(63\times 10^{-12})=0.04750
$$

$$
G+j\omega C=0.0042+j0.04750=0.04769\angle 84.95^{\circ}
$$

The two angles are identical — that is precisely what $R/L=G/C$ means geometrically. Hence:

$$
\gamma=\sqrt{(227.1\angle 84.95^{\circ})(0.04769\angle 84.95^{\circ})}=\sqrt{10.83\angle 169.90^{\circ}}=3.291\angle 84.95^{\circ}\ \checkmark
$$

$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{227.1\angle 84.95^{\circ}}{0.04769\angle 84.95^{\circ}}}=\sqrt{4762\angle 0^{\circ}}=69.0\angle 0^{\circ}\,\Omega\ \checkmark
$$

The angle subtraction gives exactly zero — which is why $Z_{0}$ is purely real on a distortionless line.

**Step 7 — What distortionless means here**

Since $\alpha=\sqrt{RG}=0.2898\,\mathrm{Np/m}$ contains no $\omega$, every frequency is attenuated equally. Since $\beta=\omega\sqrt{LC}$ is exactly proportional to $\omega$, every frequency travels at the same $2.3\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. A signal arrives smaller and later — but undistorted in shape. Note this line is still lossy ($\alpha\neq 0$); distortionless is not lossless.

questions.text: Determine the primary constants ($R$, $L$, $C$ and $G$) of a transmission line when measurement on the line at $1\,\mathrm{kHz}$ gives the following results: $Z_{0}=710\angle{-16}^{\circ}$, $\alpha=0.01\,\mathrm{neper/m}$ and $\beta=0.035\,\mathrm{rad/m}$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Recognise the strategy**

This problem runs backwards: the secondary constants are measured, and the primary ones must be recovered. The key is that $\gamma$ and $Z_{0}$ are a square root of a product and a square root of a quotient of the same two quantities. So:

$$
\gamma Z_{0}=R+j\omega L,\qquad \frac{\gamma}{Z_{0}}=G+j\omega C
$$

Multiplying kills the division; dividing kills the multiplication.

**Step 2 — Assemble $\gamma$ in polar form**

$$
\gamma=\alpha+j\beta=0.01+j0.035
$$

$$
|\gamma|=\sqrt{(0.01)^{2}+(0.035)^{2}}=\sqrt{0.0001+0.001225}=\sqrt{0.001325}=0.03640
$$

$$
\angle\gamma=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{0.035}{0.01}\right)=\tan^{-1}(3.5)=74.05^{\circ}
$$

$$
\gamma=0.03640\angle 74.05^{\circ}
$$

**Step 3 — Find $R$ and $L$**

$$
\omega=2\pi f=2\pi\times 1000=6283.2\,\mathrm{rad/s}
$$

$$
\gamma Z_{0}=(0.03640\angle 74.05^{\circ})(710\angle{-16}^{\circ})=25.844\angle 58.05^{\circ}=R+j\omega L
$$

Convert to rectangular:

$$
R=25.844\cos 58.05^{\circ}=25.844(0.5291)=13.67\,\Omega/\mathrm{m}
$$

$$
\omega L=25.844\sin 58.05^{\circ}=25.844(0.8486)=21.93
$$

$$
L=\frac{21.93}{6283.2}=3.490\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{H/m}=3.490\,\mathrm{mH/m}
$$

**Step 4 — Find $G$ and $C$**

$$
\frac{\gamma}{Z_{0}}=\frac{0.03640\angle 74.05^{\circ}}{710\angle{-16}^{\circ}}=5.127\times 10^{-5}\angle 90.05^{\circ}=G+j\omega C
$$

The angle is essentially exactly $90^{\circ}$ — which is the whole story of this problem. Converting:

$$
G=5.127\times 10^{-5}\cos 90.05^{\circ}=5.127\times 10^{-5}(-0.00095)\approx -4.9\times 10^{-8}
$$

$$
G\approx 0\,\mathrm{S/m}
$$

A negative conductance is physically impossible; the tiny value merely reflects rounding in the measured $\angle Z_{0}=-16^{\circ}$. The correct reading is $G=0$: the line has negligible shunt conductance.

$$
\omega C=5.127\times 10^{-5}\sin 90.05^{\circ}\approx 5.127\times 10^{-5}
$$

$$
C=\frac{5.127\times 10^{-5}}{6283.2}=8.160\times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F/m}=8.160\,\mathrm{nF/m}
$$

**Step 5 — Why $G=0$ was predictable**

The measurement $\angle\gamma-\angle Z_{0}=74.05^{\circ}-(-16^{\circ})=90.05^{\circ}\approx 90^{\circ}$ is not a coincidence. If $G=0$ exactly, then $G+j\omega C=j\omega C$ is purely imaginary, with angle $90^{\circ}$. Since $\gamma/Z_{0}=G+j\omega C$, reading $90^{\circ}$ there means $G=0$ — one can see it before doing any arithmetic.

**Step 6 — Verification**

Reconstruct the secondary constants from the answers:

$$
R+j\omega L=13.67+j21.93=25.84\angle 58.06^{\circ}
$$

$$
G+j\omega C=0+j5.127\times 10^{-5}=5.127\times 10^{-5}\angle 90^{\circ}
$$

$$
\gamma=\sqrt{(25.84\angle 58.06^{\circ})(5.127\times 10^{-5}\angle 90^{\circ})}=\sqrt{1.325\times 10^{-3}\angle 148.06^{\circ}}=0.0364\angle 74.03^{\circ}
$$

which in rectangular is $0.0100+j0.0350$ ✓

$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{25.84\angle 58.06^{\circ}}{5.127\times 10^{-5}\angle 90^{\circ}}}=\sqrt{504000\angle{-31.94}^{\circ}}=710\angle{-15.97}^{\circ}\ \checkmark
$$

Both match the given data.

questions.text: Define the secondary parameters of a transmission line. A lossless transmission line with $Z_{0}=50\,\Omega$ has a length of $0.4\lambda$; the operating frequency is $300\,\mathrm{MHz}$ and it is terminated with a load $Z_{L}=40+j30$. Find: (a) reflection coefficient; (b) standing wave ratio (SWR); (c) input impedance $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — The secondary parameters**

The secondary parameters of a transmission line are those derived from the four primary constants $R$, $L$, $G$, $C$, and which directly describe how a wave behaves on the line:

(i) Propagation constant $\gamma$:
$$
\gamma=\alpha+j\beta=\sqrt{(R+j\omega L)(G+j\omega C)}\quad[\mathrm{m}^{-1}]
$$
where $\alpha$ (Np/m) governs attenuation and $\beta$ (rad/m) governs phase shift.

(ii) Characteristic impedance $Z_{0}$:
$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{R+j\omega L}{G+j\omega C}}\quad[\Omega]
$$
the ratio of voltage to current of a single travelling wave — equivalently, the input impedance of an infinitely long line.

They are called secondary because they are consequences of the primary constants rather than independent properties, yet they are what one actually measures and designs with.

**Step 2 — Part (a): Reflection coefficient**

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{40+j30-50}{40+j30+50}=\frac{-10+j30}{90+j30}
$$

Rationalise by multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{(-10+j30)(90-j30)}{(90+j30)(90-j30)}
$$

Numerator:
$$
(-10)(90)+(-10)(-j30)+(j30)(90)+(j30)(-j30)=-900+j300+j2700+900=j3000
$$

(the real parts cancel exactly).

Denominator:
$$
90^{2}+30^{2}=8100+900=9000
$$

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{j3000}{9000}=j0.3333=0.3333\angle 90^{\circ}
$$

$$
|\Gamma_{L}|=0.3333
$$

**Step 3 — Part (b): Standing wave ratio**

$$
s=\frac{1+|\Gamma_{L}|}{1-|\Gamma_{L}|}=\frac{1+0.3333}{1-0.3333}=\frac{1.3333}{0.6667}=2
$$

**Step 4 — Part (c): Find $\beta\ell$**

The length is given as a fraction of a wavelength, so $\beta\ell$ follows immediately:

$$
\beta\ell=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot 0.4\lambda=0.8\pi\,\mathrm{rad}=144^{\circ}
$$

Note: the frequency $300\,\mathrm{MHz}$ is not needed. Since the length is expressed in wavelengths, $\lambda$ cancels.

$$
\tan 144^{\circ}=-0.7265
$$

**Step 5 — Apply the input impedance formula**

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{L}+jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell}{Z_{0}+jZ_{L}\tan\beta\ell}
$$

Numerator bracket:
$$
Z_{L}+jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell=40+j30+j(50)(-0.7265)=40+j30-j36.33=40-j6.33
$$

Denominator bracket: first $j(40+j30)=-30+j40$, so
$$
jZ_{L}\tan\beta\ell=(-30+j40)(-0.7265)=21.80-j29.06
$$

$$
Z_{0}+jZ_{L}\tan\beta\ell=50+21.80-j29.06=71.80-j29.06
$$

**Step 6 — Divide**

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=50\cdot\frac{40-j6.33}{71.80-j29.06}
$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $71.80+j29.06$:

Numerator:
$$
(40-j6.33)(71.80+j29.06)=2872+j1162.4-j454.5+183.9=3055.9+j707.9
$$

(using $(-j6.33)(j29.06)=+183.9$)

Denominator:
$$
(71.80)^{2}+(29.06)^{2}=5155.2+844.5=5999.7
$$

$$
\frac{40-j6.33}{71.80-j29.06}=\frac{3055.9+j707.9}{5999.7}=0.5093+j0.1180
$$

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=50(0.5093+j0.1180)=25.47+j5.90\,\Omega=26.14\angle 13.05^{\circ}\,\Omega
$$

**Step 7 — Sanity check**

The SWR computed from $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ must match the SWR at the load, since $s$ is constant along a lossless line:

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}-Z_{0}}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}+Z_{0}}=\frac{25.47+j5.90-50}{25.47+j5.90+50}=\frac{-24.53+j5.90}{75.47+j5.90}
$$

$$
|\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}|=\frac{\sqrt{(24.53)^{2}+(5.90)^{2}}}{\sqrt{(75.47)^{2}+(5.90)^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{601.7+34.8}}{\sqrt{5695.7+34.8}}=\frac{25.23}{75.70}=0.3333\ \checkmark
$$

Identical to $|\Gamma_{L}|$ — the magnitude of the reflection coefficient is unchanged along the line; only its phase rotates. Hence $s=2$ everywhere ✓
questions.answer: $\boxed{\text{Secondary: }\gamma=\sqrt{(R+j\omega L)(G+j\omega C)},\ Z_{0}=\sqrt{(R+j\omega L)/(G+j\omega C)};\ (a)\ \Gamma_{L}=j0.3333=0.3333\angle 90^{\circ};\ (b)\ s=2;\ (c)\ Z_{\mathrm{in}}=25.47+j5.90\,\Omega=26.14\angle 13.05^{\circ}\,\Omega}$

questions.text: A lossless transmission line is $80\,\mathrm{cm}$ long and operates at a frequency of $1\,\mathrm{GHz}$. The line parameters are $L=0.5\,\mu\mathrm{H/m}$ and $C=200\,\mathrm{pF/m}$. Find the characteristic impedance, the phase constant, the velocity on the line, and the input impedance for $Z_{L}=100\,\Omega$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Collect the data**

$$
\ell=80\,\mathrm{cm}=0.8\,\mathrm{m},\qquad f=1\,\mathrm{GHz}=10^{9}\,\mathrm{Hz}
$$

$$
L=0.5\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{H/m},\qquad C=200\times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}
$$

$$
\omega=2\pi f=6.2832\times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{rad/s},\qquad R=G=0\ \text{(lossless)}
$$

**Step 2 — Characteristic impedance**

For a lossless line $Z_{0}$ is purely real:

$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.5\times 10^{-6}}{200\times 10^{-12}}}=\sqrt{2500}=50\,\Omega
$$

**Step 3 — Velocity**

$$
LC=(0.5\times 10^{-6})(200\times 10^{-12})=1\times 10^{-16}
$$

$$
\sqrt{LC}=10^{-8}
$$

$$
u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}=\frac{1}{10^{-8}}=10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}
$$

(about one-third the speed of light).

**Step 4 — Phase constant**

$$
\beta=\omega\sqrt{LC}=(6.2832\times 10^{9})(10^{-8})=62.83\,\mathrm{rad/m}
$$

Check: $\beta=\omega/u=(6.2832\times 10^{9})/10^{8}=62.83\,\mathrm{rad/m}$ ✓

**Step 5 — Electrical length: look before computing**

$$
\lambda=\frac{u}{f}=\frac{10^{8}}{10^{9}}=0.1\,\mathrm{m}=10\,\mathrm{cm}
$$

$$
\frac{\ell}{\lambda}=\frac{0.8}{0.1}=8
$$

The line is exactly $8$ wavelengths long. Since $8\lambda=16\times(\lambda/2)$, it is an integer number of half-wavelengths — and a half-wave line repeats its load impedance. So the answer can be written down without any arithmetic:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{L}=100\,\Omega
$$

**Step 6 — Confirm with the formula**

$$
\beta\ell=(62.83)(0.8)=50.27\,\mathrm{rad}
$$

Reduce modulo $2\pi$: $50.27/(2\pi)=50.27/6.2832=8.000$, so $\beta\ell=8\times 2\pi$ exactly, an integer number of full revolutions:

$$
\tan\beta\ell=\tan(16\pi)=0
$$

Substituting into the input impedance formula:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{L}+jZ_{0}(0)}{Z_{0}+jZ_{L}(0)}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{L}}{Z_{0}}=Z_{L}=100\,\Omega
$$

**Step 7 — Remark**

This illustrates why electrical length matters more than physical length. An $80\,\mathrm{cm}$ line is electrically invisible at $1\,\mathrm{GHz}$ (given these parameters), yet at, say, $1.03\,\mathrm{GHz}$ the same physical line would present something quite different. Note also that the line is not matched ($Z_{L}=100\neq 50=Z_{0}$), so reflections certainly exist:

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{100-50}{100+50}=\frac{1}{3},\qquad s=\frac{1+1/3}{1-1/3}=2
$$

The reflections are present all along the line — it is only at the input plane, after a whole number of half-wavelengths, that the phase has rotated fully back and $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ happens to equal $Z_{L}$.

questions.text: What is a distortionless transmission line? Why are telephone lines required to be distortionless?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Definition**

A distortionless line is one on which a signal’s shape is preserved as it travels: every frequency component is attenuated by the same amount and travels at the same speed. The signal arrives smaller and later, but not misshapen.

The condition for this is a relation among the primary constants:

$$
\frac{R}{L}=\frac{G}{C}\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad RC=LG
$$

**Step 2 — Why this condition produces the result**

Let $k=R/L=G/C$. Then

$$
R+j\omega L=L(k+j\omega),\qquad G+j\omega C=C(k+j\omega)
$$

The same complex factor $(k+j\omega)$ appears in both — and that is the whole trick.

$$
\gamma=\sqrt{L(k+j\omega)\cdot C(k+j\omega)}=(k+j\omega)\sqrt{LC}
$$

Separating real and imaginary parts:

$$
\alpha=k\sqrt{LC}=\sqrt{RG},\qquad \beta=\omega\sqrt{LC}
$$

and in the quotient the factor cancels outright:

$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{L(k+j\omega)}{C(k+j\omega)}}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}
$$

**Step 3 — The three consequences**

| Quantity | Result | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| $\alpha=\sqrt{RG}$ | independent of $\omega$ | all frequencies attenuated equally $\Rightarrow$ no amplitude distortion |
| $\beta=\omega\sqrt{LC}$ | proportional to $\omega$ | $u=\omega/\beta=1/\sqrt{LC}$ is constant $\Rightarrow$ no phase (delay) distortion |
| $Z_{0}=\sqrt{L/C}$ | real, independent of $\omega$ | matching works at all frequencies |

Important: distortionless is not lossless. A distortionless line still attenuates ($\alpha=\sqrt{RG}\neq 0$); it simply attenuates everything equally. A lossless line ($R=G=0$) is a special case, since $0/L=0/C$ is satisfied trivially.

**Step 4 — Why telephone lines must be distortionless**

Speech is not a single tone: it occupies a band of roughly $300\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to $3.4\,\mathrm{kHz}$, and its intelligibility depends on the precise relative amplitudes and timings of those components.

On an ordinary line, $\alpha$ and $u$ both vary with frequency. The consequences for speech are severe:

- **Amplitude distortion:** high frequencies are attenuated more than low ones. Since consonants ($s$, $f$, $th$) live in the upper band, speech becomes muffled and words are confused.
- **Delay distortion:** components travel at different speeds, so they arrive at different times. A sharp sound smears out; syllables run together.

The result is a waveform that is no longer a scaled copy of what was spoken — it is a different waveform, and beyond a certain length the speech becomes unintelligible.

Making the line distortionless guarantees that

$$
v_{\mathrm{out}}(t)=K\,v_{\mathrm{in}}(t-t_{d})
$$

that is, the output is the input merely scaled by $K=e^{-\alpha\ell}$ and delayed by $t_{d}=\ell/u$. Both are harmless: scaling is fixed by an amplifier, and a uniform delay is imperceptible. What matters is that the shape survives.

**Step 5 — A historical note**

Real cables have $R/L\gg G/C$, because $L$ is naturally small and $R$ is not. There are four ways to force the equality — decrease $R$, decrease $C$, increase $G$, or increase $L$ — and only the last is practical: reducing $R$ means more copper, reducing $C$ is limited by geometry, and increasing $G$ deliberately adds loss.

Oliver Heaviside deduced this condition theoretically in the 1880s and proposed adding series inductance. The idea was implemented as loading coils (Pupin coils), inserted at regular intervals along telephone lines — and it transformed long-distance telephony, extending usable range dramatically.

questions.text: A lossless $50\,\Omega$ line is $1.5\lambda$ long and is terminated with a pure resistance of $100\,\Omega$. The load voltage is $40\angle 60^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}$. Find: (a) the average power delivered to the load; (b) the magnitude of the minimum voltage on the line.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Part (a): Average power delivered to the load**

The load is a pure resistance, so the power follows directly from the load voltage:

$$
P_{L}=\frac{|V_{L}|^{2}}{2R_{L}}=\frac{(40)^{2}}{2(100)}=\frac{1600}{200}=8\,\mathrm{W}
$$

The phase angle $60^{\circ}$ is irrelevant to power — only the magnitude matters. The factor of $2$ converts the peak amplitude to RMS.

**Step 2 — Part (b): Reflection coefficient**

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{100-50}{100+50}=\frac{50}{150}=\frac{1}{3}=0.3333
$$

Note it is real and positive. That is significant: it means the load sits exactly at a voltage maximum.

**Step 3 — Find the forward-wave amplitude**

At the load,

$$
V_{L}=V_{0}^{+}(1+\Gamma_{L})=V_{0}^{+}\!\left(1+\frac{1}{3}\right)=V_{0}^{+}\cdot\frac{4}{3}
$$

$$
|V_{0}^{+}|=|V_{L}|\cdot\frac{3}{4}=40\times\frac{3}{4}=30\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 4 — Minimum voltage**

$$
|V|_{\min}=|V_{0}^{+}|(1-|\Gamma_{L}|)=30\!\left(1-\frac{1}{3}\right)=30\times\frac{2}{3}=20\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 5 — Verification**

$$
|V|_{\max}=|V_{0}^{+}|(1+|\Gamma_{L}|)=30\times\frac{4}{3}=40\,\mathrm{V}
$$

which equals $|V_{L}|$ ✓ — confirming the load is at a maximum, as predicted from $\Gamma_{L}>0$.

$$
s=\frac{1+1/3}{1-1/3}=\frac{4/3}{2/3}=2,\qquad \frac{|V|_{\max}}{|V|_{\min}}=\frac{40}{20}=2\ \checkmark
$$

**Step 6 — On the line length**

The length $1.5\lambda$ is not needed for either part. It matters only in that $1.5\lambda=3\times(\lambda/2)$ contains three complete standing-wave periods, so minima certainly occur on the line. (It also means $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{L}$, though that is not asked.)

questions.text: A lossless $60\,\Omega$ line is $1.8\lambda$ long and is terminated with a pure resistance of $80\,\Omega$. The load voltage is $15\angle 30^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}$. Find: (i) average power delivered to the load; (ii) magnitude of minimum voltage on the line.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Part (i): Average power delivered to the load**

$$
P_{L}=\frac{|V_{L}|^{2}}{2R_{L}}=\frac{(15)^{2}}{2(80)}=\frac{225}{160}=1.406\,\mathrm{W}
$$

**Step 2 — Part (ii): Reflection coefficient**

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{80-60}{80+60}=\frac{20}{140}=\frac{1}{7}=0.1429
$$

Real and positive again, so the load lies at a voltage maximum.

**Step 3 — Forward-wave amplitude**

$$
V_{L}=V_{0}^{+}(1+\Gamma_{L})=V_{0}^{+}\!\left(1+\frac{1}{7}\right)=V_{0}^{+}\cdot\frac{8}{7}
$$

$$
|V_{0}^{+}|=15\times\frac{7}{8}=13.125\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 4 — Minimum voltage**

$$
|V|_{\min}=|V_{0}^{+}|(1-|\Gamma_{L}|)=13.125\!\left(1-\frac{1}{7}\right)=13.125\times\frac{6}{7}=11.25\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 5 — Verification**

$$
s=\frac{1+1/7}{1-1/7}=\frac{8/7}{6/7}=\frac{8}{6}=1.333
$$

$$
\frac{|V|_{\max}}{|V|_{\min}}=\frac{15}{11.25}=1.333\ \checkmark
$$

The SWR is close to $1$ because $Z_{L}=80$ is not far from $Z_{0}=60$ — a nearly matched line, with only a shallow standing-wave ripple.

questions.text: A $200\,\Omega$ transmission line is lossless, $0.25\lambda$ long and is terminated in $Z_{L}=400\,\Omega$. The line has the generator with $80\angle 0^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}$ in series with $100\,\Omega$ connected to the input. (a) Find the load voltage; (b) find the voltage at the midpoint of the line.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Input impedance: recognise the quarter-wave line**

The line is $0.25\lambda=\lambda/4$ long, so it is a quarter-wave transformer:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{Z_{0}^{2}}{Z_{L}}=\frac{(200)^{2}}{400}=\frac{40000}{400}=100\,\Omega
$$

**Step 2 — Input voltage by the voltage divider**

The generator sees only $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$:

$$
V_{\mathrm{in}}=V_{g}\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}}{Z_{g}+Z_{\mathrm{in}}}=80\times\frac{100}{100+100}=80(0.5)=40\angle 0^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 3 — Set up the travelling-wave description**

Place the load at $d=0$ and measure $d$ back toward the generator:

$$
V(d)=V_{0}^{+}\!\left(e^{j\beta d}+\Gamma_{L}e^{-j\beta d}\right)
$$

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{400-200}{400+200}=\frac{200}{600}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

At the input, $d=\ell=\lambda/4$, so

$$
\beta\ell=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{\lambda}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}=90^{\circ}
$$

$$
e^{j\beta\ell}=e^{j\pi/2}=j,\qquad e^{-j\beta\ell}=-j
$$

**Step 4 — Solve for $V_{0}^{+}$**

$$
V_{\mathrm{in}}=V_{0}^{+}\!\left(j+\frac{1}{3}(-j)\right)=V_{0}^{+}\,j\!\left(1-\frac{1}{3}\right)=V_{0}^{+}\,j\cdot\frac{2}{3}
$$

$$
40=V_{0}^{+}\cdot\frac{2j}{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_{0}^{+}=40\times\frac{3}{2j}=\frac{60}{j}=-j60=60\angle{-90}^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 5 — Part (a): Load voltage**

$$
V_{L}=V_{0}^{+}(1+\Gamma_{L})=(60\angle{-90}^{\circ})\!\left(1+\frac{1}{3}\right)=(60\angle{-90}^{\circ})\cdot\frac{4}{3}=80\angle{-90}^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}=-j80\,\mathrm{V}
$$

Check by power conservation. The line is lossless, so all power entering must arrive:

$$
P_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{|V_{\mathrm{in}}|^{2}}{2Z_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{(40)^{2}}{2(100)}=8\,\mathrm{W}
$$

$$
P_{L}=\frac{|V_{L}|^{2}}{2Z_{L}}=\frac{(80)^{2}}{2(400)}=\frac{6400}{800}=8\,\mathrm{W}\ \checkmark
$$

An exact match — a strong confirmation of $V_{L}$.

**Step 6 — Part (b): Voltage at the midpoint**

The midpoint is at $d=\ell/2=\lambda/8$ from the load:

$$
\beta d=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{\lambda}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4}=45^{\circ}
$$

$$
V\!\left(\frac{\lambda}{8}\right)=V_{0}^{+}\!\left(e^{j\pi/4}+\frac{1}{3}e^{-j\pi/4}\right)
$$

**Step 7 — Evaluate the bracket**

$$
e^{j\pi/4}=0.7071+j0.7071
$$

$$
\frac{1}{3}e^{-j\pi/4}=\frac{1}{3}(0.7071-j0.7071)=0.2357-j0.2357
$$

Adding:
$$
0.7071+0.2357+j(0.7071-0.2357)=0.9428+j0.4714
$$

$$
|\,|= \sqrt{(0.9428)^{2}+(0.4714)^{2}}=\sqrt{0.8889+0.2222}=\sqrt{1.1111}=1.0541
$$

$$
\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{0.4714}{0.9428}\right)=\tan^{-1}(0.5)=26.57^{\circ}
$$

**Step 8 — The midpoint voltage**

$$
V_{\mathrm{mid}}=(60\angle{-90}^{\circ})(1.0541\angle 26.57^{\circ})=63.25\angle{-63.43}^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 9 — Sanity check on the range**

$$
|V|_{\max}=|V_{0}^{+}|(1+|\Gamma_{L}|)=60\times\frac{4}{3}=80\,\mathrm{V}
$$

$$
|V|_{\min}=|V_{0}^{+}|(1-|\Gamma_{L}|)=60\times\frac{2}{3}=40\,\mathrm{V}
$$

The voltage on this line can only lie between $40$ and $80\,\mathrm{V}$. Our three values fit: $|V_{L}|=80$ (a maximum, since $\Gamma_{L}>0$), $|V_{\mathrm{in}}|=40$ (a minimum — a quarter wave away, exactly as it must be), and $|V_{\mathrm{mid}}|=63.25$, comfortably between ✓

questions.text: A lossless $50\,\Omega$ line, $0.4\lambda$ long, is terminated with a load $Z_{L}=40+j30\,\Omega$. If the operating frequency is $300\,\mathrm{MHz}$, find: (a) reflection coefficient $\Gamma$; (b) standing wave ratio ($s$); (c) input impedance $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$.
questions.solution:
**Step 0 — Note**

This is the same problem as Question 4 of the preceding section (there set in 2079 Bhadra), with identical data. It is solved again here in full, since it appears independently in the papers.

**Step 1 — Part (a): Reflection coefficient**

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{40+j30-50}{40+j30+50}=\frac{-10+j30}{90+j30}
$$

Multiply above and below by the conjugate $90-j30$:

Numerator $=(-10+j30)(90-j30)=-900+j300+j2700+900=j3000$ (the real parts cancel exactly)

Denominator $=90^{2}+30^{2}=9000$

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{j3000}{9000}=j0.3333=0.3333\angle 90^{\circ}
$$

**Step 2 — Part (b): Standing wave ratio**

$$
s=\frac{1+|\Gamma_{L}|}{1-|\Gamma_{L}|}=\frac{1+0.3333}{1-0.3333}=\frac{1.3333}{0.6667}=2
$$

**Step 3 — Part (c): Electrical length**

$$
\beta\ell=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot 0.4\lambda=0.8\pi=144^{\circ},\qquad \tan 144^{\circ}=-0.7265
$$

The frequency $300\,\mathrm{MHz}$ is not needed — the length is given in wavelengths, so $\lambda$ cancels.

**Step 4 — Input impedance**

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{L}+jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell}{Z_{0}+jZ_{L}\tan\beta\ell}
$$

Numerator bracket:
$$
40+j30+j(50)(-0.7265)=40+j30-j36.33=40-j6.33
$$

Denominator bracket: first $j(40+j30)=-30+j40$, so
$$
50+(-30+j40)(-0.7265)=50+21.80-j29.06=71.80-j29.06
$$

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=50\cdot\frac{40-j6.33}{71.80-j29.06}
$$

Rationalising with the conjugate $71.80+j29.06$:

Numerator $=(40-j6.33)(71.80+j29.06)=3055.9+j707.9$

Denominator $=(71.80)^{2}+(29.06)^{2}=5999.7$

$$
\frac{40-j6.33}{71.80-j29.06}=0.5093+j0.1180
$$

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=50(0.5093+j0.1180)=25.47+j5.90\,\Omega=26.14\angle 13.05^{\circ}\,\Omega
$$

questions.text: A lossless transmission line with $Z_{0}=50\,\Omega$ is $30\,\mathrm{m}$ long and operates at $2\,\mathrm{MHz}$. The line is terminated with a load $Z_{L}=(60+j40)\,\Omega$ and velocity $v=3\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find: (a) the reflection coefficient; (b) the standing wave ratio and the input impedance.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Electrical length**

Here the length is in metres, so the wavelength is needed:

$$
\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{3\times 10^{8}}{2\times 10^{6}}=150\,\mathrm{m}
$$

$$
\frac{\ell}{\lambda}=\frac{30}{150}=0.2
$$

$$
\beta\ell=2\pi(0.2)=0.4\pi=1.2566\,\mathrm{rad}=72^{\circ},\qquad \tan 72^{\circ}=3.0777
$$

**Step 2 — Part (a): Reflection coefficient**

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{60+j40-50}{60+j40+50}=\frac{10+j40}{110+j40}
$$

Rationalise with the conjugate $110-j40$:

Numerator $=(10+j40)(110-j40)=1100-j400+j4400+1600=2700+j4000$

Denominator $=110^{2}+40^{2}=12100+1600=13700$

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{2700+j4000}{13700}=0.1971+j0.2920
$$

$$
|\Gamma_{L}|=\sqrt{(0.1971)^{2}+(0.2920)^{2}}=\sqrt{0.03884+0.08525}=\sqrt{0.12409}=0.3523
$$

$$
\angle\Gamma_{L}=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{0.2920}{0.1971}\right)=55.98^{\circ}
$$

$$
\Gamma_{L}=0.1971+j0.2920=0.3523\angle 55.98^{\circ}
$$

**Step 3 — Part (b): Standing wave ratio**

$$
s=\frac{1+|\Gamma_{L}|}{1-|\Gamma_{L}|}=\frac{1+0.3523}{1-0.3523}=\frac{1.3523}{0.6477}=2.088
$$

**Step 4 — Input impedance**

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{L}+jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell}{Z_{0}+jZ_{L}\tan\beta\ell}
$$

Numerator bracket:
$$
60+j40+j(50)(3.0777)=60+j40+j153.88=60+j193.88
$$

Denominator bracket: first $j(60+j40)=-40+j60$, so
$$
50+(-40+j60)(3.0777)=50-123.11+j184.66=-73.11+j184.66
$$

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=50\cdot\frac{60+j193.88}{-73.11+j184.66}
$$

**Step 5 — Divide in polar form**

$$
60+j193.88=\sqrt{3600+37590}=\sqrt{41190}=202.95,\quad\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{193.88}{60}\right)=72.80^{\circ}
$$

$$
|-73.11+j184.66|=\sqrt{5345+34099}=\sqrt{39444}=198.61
$$

The denominator lies in the second quadrant (negative real, positive imaginary), so

$$
\angle=180^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{184.66}{73.11}\right)=180^{\circ}-68.40^{\circ}=111.60^{\circ}
$$

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=50\times\frac{202.95\angle 72.80^{\circ}}{198.61\angle 111.60^{\circ}}=50\times 1.0219\angle{-38.80}^{\circ}
$$

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=51.10\angle{-38.80}^{\circ}\,\Omega=39.82-j32.01\,\Omega
$$

**Step 6 — Check**

The magnitude of the reflection coefficient must be unchanged at the input (lossless line):

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}-Z_{0}}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}+Z_{0}}=\frac{39.82-j32.01-50}{39.82-j32.01+50}=\frac{-10.18-j32.01}{89.82-j32.01}
$$

$$
|\Gamma_{\mathrm{in}}|=\frac{\sqrt{103.6+1024.6}}{\sqrt{8067.6+1024.6}}=\frac{\sqrt{1128.2}}{\sqrt{9092.2}}=\frac{33.59}{95.35}=0.3523\ \checkmark
$$

identical to $|\Gamma_{L}|$ — only the phase has rotated.

questions.text: A lossless transmission line with $Z_{0}=50\,\Omega$ and length $1.5\,\mathrm{m}$ connects a voltage source $V_{g}=60\,\mathrm{V}$ to a terminal load $Z_{L}=(50+j50)\,\Omega$. If the operating frequency $f=100\,\mathrm{MHz}$, generator impedance $Z_{g}=50\,\Omega$ and speed of wave equal to the speed of light, find the distance of the first voltage maximum from the load, and the power delivered to the load.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Electrical length: a half-wave line**

$$
\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{3\times 10^{8}}{100\times 10^{6}}=3\,\mathrm{m}
$$

$$
\frac{\ell}{\lambda}=\frac{1.5}{3}=0.5
$$

The line is exactly half a wavelength long. By the half-wave repeater property:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{L}=50+j50\,\Omega
$$

$$
\beta=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}=\frac{2\pi}{3}=2.0944\,\mathrm{rad/m}
$$

**Step 2 — Reflection coefficient**

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{50+j50-50}{50+j50+50}=\frac{j50}{100+j50}
$$

In polar form:

$$
j50=50\angle 90^{\circ}
$$

$$
100+j50=\sqrt{10000+2500}\angle\tan^{-1}(0.5)=111.80\angle 26.57^{\circ}
$$

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{50\angle 90^{\circ}}{111.80\angle 26.57^{\circ}}=0.4472\angle 63.43^{\circ}
$$

So $|\Gamma_{L}|=0.4472$, $\phi=63.43^{\circ}=1.1071\,\mathrm{rad}$.

**Step 3 — Distance of the first voltage maximum**

Writing the voltage at distance $d$ from the load and factoring out $e^{j\beta d}$:

$$
V(d)=V_{0}^{+}\!\left(e^{j\beta d}+\Gamma_{L}e^{-j\beta d}\right)=V_{0}^{+}e^{j\beta d}\!\left(1+|\Gamma_{L}|e^{j(\phi-2\beta d)}\right)
$$

The magnitude is greatest when the two terms in the bracket align, i.e. when the exponent vanishes:

$$
\phi-2\beta d=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_{\max}=\frac{\phi}{2\beta}
$$

$$
d_{\max}=\frac{1.1071}{2(2.0944)}=\frac{1.1071}{4.1888}=0.2643\,\mathrm{m}=26.4\,\mathrm{cm}
$$

Check by proportion: a full $360^{\circ}$ of the angle $\phi-2\beta d$ corresponds to $\lambda/2$ of travel, so

$$
d_{\max}=\frac{63.43^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}}\times\frac{\lambda}{2}=0.1762\times 1.5=0.2643\,\mathrm{m}\ \checkmark
$$

**Step 4 — Input voltage**

Since $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{L}=50+j50$, the voltage divider gives

$$
V_{\mathrm{in}}=V_{g}\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}}{Z_{g}+Z_{\mathrm{in}}}=60\times\frac{50+j50}{50+50+j50}=60\times\frac{50+j50}{100+j50}
$$

Rationalise:
$$
\frac{50+j50}{100+j50}=\frac{(50+j50)(100-j50)}{10000+2500}=\frac{5000-j2500+j5000+2500}{12500}=\frac{7500+j2500}{12500}=0.6+j0.2
$$

$$
V_{\mathrm{in}}=60(0.6+j0.2)=36+j12\,\mathrm{V}
$$

$$
|V_{\mathrm{in}}|=\sqrt{1296+144}=\sqrt{1440}=37.95\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 5 — Power**

Since the line is lossless, the power entering the input equals the power reaching the load. Use $P=\tfrac{1}{2}|I_{\mathrm{in}}|^{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\{Z_{\mathrm{in}}\}$.

First find the input current:

$$
I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{36+j12}{50+j50}=\frac{(36+j12)(50-j50)}{2500+2500}=\frac{1800-j1800+j600+600}{5000}=\frac{2400-j1200}{5000}
$$

$$
I_{\mathrm{in}}=0.48-j0.24\,\mathrm{A}
$$

$$
|I_{\mathrm{in}}|^{2}=(0.48)^{2}+(0.24)^{2}=0.2304+0.0576=0.288
$$

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}(0.288)(50)=7.2\,\mathrm{W}
$$

**Step 6 — Verification by a second route**

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}|V_{\mathrm{in}}|^{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left\{\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}^{*}}\right\}
$$

With $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=70.71\angle 45^{\circ}$, we have $Z_{\mathrm{in}}^{*}=70.71\angle{-45}^{\circ}$ and

$$
\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}^{*}}=0.014142\angle 45^{\circ}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm{Re}=0.014142(0.7071)=0.01
$$

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}(1440)(0.01)=7.2\,\mathrm{W}\ \checkmark
$$

Note that only the real part of $Z_{L}$ absorbs power; the reactive part merely stores and returns it each cycle.

questions.text: A two-wire $40\,\Omega$ line ($Z_{0}=40\,\Omega$) connecting a source of $80\,\mathrm{V}$, $400\,\mathrm{kHz}$ with series resistance $10\,\Omega$ to a load of $Z_{L}=60\,\Omega$. The line is $75\,\mathrm{m}$ long and the velocity on the line is $2.5\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Find the voltage $V_{\mathrm{in},s}$ at the input end and $V_{L,s}$ at the output end of the transmission line.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Electrical length**

$$
\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{2.5\times 10^{8}}{400\times 10^{3}}=625\,\mathrm{m}
$$

$$
\frac{\ell}{\lambda}=\frac{75}{625}=0.12
$$

$$
\beta\ell=2\pi(0.12)=0.7540\,\mathrm{rad}=43.2^{\circ},\qquad \tan 43.2^{\circ}=0.9387
$$

**Step 2 — Input impedance**

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{L}+jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell}{Z_{0}+jZ_{L}\tan\beta\ell}=40\cdot\frac{60+j(40)(0.9387)}{40+j(60)(0.9387)}=40\cdot\frac{60+j37.55}{40+j56.32}
$$

In polar form:

$$
60+j37.55=\sqrt{3600+1410}=70.78,\quad\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{37.55}{60}\right)=32.02^{\circ}
$$

$$
40+j56.32=\sqrt{1600+3172}=69.08,\quad\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{56.32}{40}\right)=54.62^{\circ}
$$

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=40\times\frac{70.78\angle 32.02^{\circ}}{69.08\angle 54.62^{\circ}}=40\times 1.0246\angle{-22.60}^{\circ}=40.98\angle{-22.60}^{\circ}
$$

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=37.84-j15.75\,\Omega
$$

**Step 3 — Input voltage**

$$
V_{\mathrm{in},s}=V_{g}\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}}{Z_{g}+Z_{\mathrm{in}}}=80\times\frac{37.84-j15.75}{10+37.84-j15.75}=80\times\frac{37.84-j15.75}{47.84-j15.75}
$$

$$
|47.84-j15.75|=\sqrt{2288+248}=50.36,\quad\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{-15.75}{47.84}\right)=-18.23^{\circ}
$$

$$
V_{\mathrm{in},s}=80\times\frac{40.98\angle{-22.60}^{\circ}}{50.36\angle{-18.23}^{\circ}}=80\times 0.8138\angle{-4.37}^{\circ}
$$

$$
V_{\mathrm{in},s}=65.10\angle{-4.37}^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 4 — Find the forward-wave amplitude**

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{60-40}{60+40}=\frac{20}{100}=0.2
$$

At the input, $d=\ell$ and $\beta\ell=43.2^{\circ}$:

$$
V_{\mathrm{in},s}=V_{0}^{+}\!\left(e^{j43.2^{\circ}}+0.2\,e^{-j43.2^{\circ}}\right)
$$

Evaluate the bracket:

$$
e^{j43.2^{\circ}}=0.7290+j0.6845
$$

$$
0.2\,e^{-j43.2^{\circ}}=0.1458-j0.1369
$$

$$
\text{Sum}=0.8749+j0.5476
$$

$$
|\,|=\sqrt{0.7654+0.2999}=\sqrt{1.0653}=1.0321,\quad\angle=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{0.5476}{0.8749}\right)=32.03^{\circ}
$$

$$
V_{0}^{+}=\frac{65.10\angle{-4.37}^{\circ}}{1.0321\angle 32.03^{\circ}}=63.08\angle{-36.40}^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 5 — Load voltage**

$$
V_{L,s}=V_{0}^{+}(1+\Gamma_{L})=(63.08\angle{-36.40}^{\circ})(1+0.2)=(63.08\angle{-36.40}^{\circ})(1.2)
$$

$$
V_{L,s}=75.69\angle{-36.40}^{\circ}\,\mathrm{V}
$$

**Step 6 — Verification by power conservation**

The line is lossless, so the input and load powers must agree.

$$
P_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{1}{2}|V_{\mathrm{in},s}|^{2}\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left\{\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}^{*}}\right\}
$$

With $Z_{\mathrm{in}}^{*}=40.98\angle 22.60^{\circ}$:

$$
\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}^{*}}=0.02440\angle{-22.60}^{\circ}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm{Re}=0.02440(0.9232)=0.02253
$$

$$
P_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{1}{2}(65.10)^{2}(0.02253)=\frac{1}{2}(4238)(0.02253)=47.7\,\mathrm{W}
$$

$$
P_{L}=\frac{|V_{L,s}|^{2}}{2R_{L}}=\frac{(75.69)^{2}}{2(60)}=\frac{5729}{120}=47.7\,\mathrm{W}\ \checkmark
$$

The two agree — confirming both voltages at once.

Note that $|V_{L,s}|=75.69\,\mathrm{V}$ exceeds $|V_{\mathrm{in},s}|=65.10\,\mathrm{V}$. There is no contradiction: on a mismatched line the standing-wave pattern makes the voltage vary along the line, and the load here happens to sit near a maximum (since $\Gamma_{L}>0$).

questions.text: The velocity of propagation on a lossless transmission line is $2.5\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. If the capacitance of the line is $30\,\mathrm{pF/m}$, find: (a) inductance of the line; (b) characteristic impedance; (c) phase constant at $100\,\mathrm{MHz}$; (d) reflection coefficient if the line is terminated with a resistive load of $50\,\Omega$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — Part (a): Inductance**

For a lossless line:

$$
v=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad LC=\frac{1}{v^{2}}
$$

$$
LC=\frac{1}{(2.5\times 10^{8})^{2}}=\frac{1}{6.25\times 10^{16}}=1.6\times 10^{-17}
$$

$$
L=\frac{1.6\times 10^{-17}}{30\times 10^{-12}}=5.333\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{H/m}=0.533\,\mu\mathrm{H/m}
$$

**Step 2 — Part (b): Characteristic impedance**

$$
Z_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}=\sqrt{\frac{5.333\times 10^{-7}}{30\times 10^{-12}}}=\sqrt{17778}=133.3\,\Omega
$$

Check by a neat shortcut. Combining $v=1/\sqrt{LC}$ with $Z_{0}=\sqrt{L/C}$ gives

$$
Z_{0}=\frac{1}{vC}
$$

(since $1/(vC)=\sqrt{LC}/C=\sqrt{L/C}$). Hence

$$
Z_{0}=\frac{1}{(2.5\times 10^{8})(30\times 10^{-12})}=\frac{1}{7.5\times 10^{-3}}=133.3\,\Omega\ \checkmark
$$

— the answer in one step, without finding $L$ at all.

**Step 3 — Part (c): Phase constant at $100\,\mathrm{MHz}$**

$$
\omega=2\pi f=2\pi\times 100\times 10^{6}=6.2832\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{rad/s}
$$

$$
\beta=\frac{\omega}{v}=\frac{6.2832\times 10^{8}}{2.5\times 10^{8}}=2.513\,\mathrm{rad/m}
$$

Check: $\lambda=v/f=(2.5\times 10^{8})/(100\times 10^{6})=2.5\,\mathrm{m}$, and $\beta=2\pi/\lambda=2\pi/2.5=2.513\,\mathrm{rad/m}$ ✓

**Step 4 — Part (d): Reflection coefficient**

$$
\Gamma_{L}=\frac{Z_{L}-Z_{0}}{Z_{L}+Z_{0}}=\frac{50-133.3}{50+133.3}=\frac{-83.3}{183.3}=-0.4545
$$

It is real and negative because $Z_{L}<Z_{0}$: the reflected wave returns inverted ($180^{\circ}$ phase reversal), and the load sits at a voltage minimum.

$$
s=\frac{1+0.4545}{1-0.4545}=\frac{1.4545}{0.5455}=2.667
