$$

questions.text: Derive the expression for the input impedance of a transmission line with characteristic impedance $Z_{0}$, excited by source $V$ with source impedance $Z_{s}$ and terminated in load $Z_{l}$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — The general solution on a line**

The voltage and current on a transmission line consist of a forward and a backward travelling wave. Measuring distance $d$ from the load back toward the source:

$$
V(d)=V_{0}^{+}e^{\gamma d}+V_{0}^{-}e^{-\gamma d}
$$

$$
I(d)=\frac{1}{Z_{0}}\left(V_{0}^{+}e^{\gamma d}-V_{0}^{-}e^{-\gamma d}\right)
$$

The minus sign in the current is essential: the backward wave carries power the other way, so its current reverses relative to its voltage. ($Z_{0}$ is defined as the voltage-to-current ratio of a single travelling wave.)

**Step 2 — Apply the load condition**

At the load, $d=0$:

$$
V_{L}=V_{0}^{+}+V_{0}^{-},\qquad I_{L}=\frac{1}{Z_{0}}(V_{0}^{+}-V_{0}^{-})
$$

Solving these two simultaneously for the wave amplitudes:

$$
V_{0}^{+}=\frac{V_{L}+Z_{0}I_{L}}{2},\qquad V_{0}^{-}=\frac{V_{L}-Z_{0}I_{L}}{2}
$$

**Step 3 — Evaluate at the input, $d=\ell$**

$$
V_{\mathrm{in}}=V_{0}^{+}e^{\gamma\ell}+V_{0}^{-}e^{-\gamma\ell}=\frac{V_{L}+Z_{0}I_{L}}{2}e^{\gamma\ell}+\frac{V_{L}-Z_{0}I_{L}}{2}e^{-\gamma\ell}
$$

Regroup by collecting the $V_{L}$ and $I_{L}$ terms:

$$
V_{\mathrm{in}}=V_{L}\cosh\gamma\ell+Z_{0}I_{L}\sinh\gamma\ell
$$

Identically for the current:

$$
I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{1}{Z_{0}}\left(V_{0}^{+}e^{\gamma\ell}-V_{0}^{-}e^{-\gamma\ell}\right)=\frac{V_{L}}{Z_{0}}\sinh\gamma\ell+I_{L}\cosh\gamma\ell
$$

**Step 4 — Form the ratio**

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{I_{\mathrm{in}}}=\frac{V_{L}\cosh\gamma\ell+Z_{0}I_{L}\sinh\gamma\ell}{(V_{L}/Z_{0})\sinh\gamma\ell+I_{L}\cosh\gamma\ell}
$$

Divide numerator and denominator by $I_{L}$, and substitute $V_{L}=Z_{l}I_{L}$:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{Z_{l}\cosh\gamma\ell+Z_{0}\sinh\gamma\ell}{(Z_{l}/Z_{0})\sinh\gamma\ell+\cosh\gamma\ell}
$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by $Z_{0}$:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{l}\cosh\gamma\ell+Z_{0}\sinh\gamma\ell}{Z_{0}\cosh\gamma\ell+Z_{l}\sinh\gamma\ell}
$$

Finally divide through by $\cosh\gamma\ell$:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{l}+Z_{0}\tanh\gamma\ell}{Z_{0}+Z_{l}\tanh\gamma\ell}
$$

**Step 5 — The lossless case**

For a lossless line $\alpha=0$, so $\gamma=j\beta$. Using $\tanh(j\theta)=j\tan\theta$:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_{0}\frac{Z_{l}+jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell}{Z_{0}+jZ_{l}\tan\beta\ell}
$$

**Step 6 — The role of the source**

Note carefully what the derivation shows: $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ does not depend on $V$ or $Z_{s}$ at all. It is determined solely by $Z_{0}$, $Z_{l}$ and the electrical length $\gamma\ell$. The source affects only the amplitude of the waves, never the impedance the line presents.

Once $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ is known, the entire line and load collapse to a single lumped impedance, and the input conditions follow from an ordinary voltage divider:

$$
V_{\mathrm{in}}=V\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}}{Z_{s}+Z_{\mathrm{in}}},\qquad I_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{V}{Z_{s}+Z_{\mathrm{in}}}
$$

This is what makes $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ so useful: it is the bridge between distributed field theory and ordinary circuit theory.

**Step 7 — Special cases (all read off the boxed formula)**

| Condition | $Z_{\mathrm{in}}$ | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| $Z_{l}=Z_{0}$ | $Z_{0}$ | numerator and denominator share the factor |
| $\ell=n\lambda/2$ | $Z_{l}$ | $\tan\beta\ell=0$ |
| $\ell=\lambda/4$ | $Z_{0}^{2}/Z_{l}$ | $\tan\beta\ell\to\infty$ |
| $Z_{l}=0$ (short) | $jZ_{0}\tan\beta\ell$ | purely reactive |
| $Z_{l}=\infty$ (open) | $-jZ_{0}\cot\beta\ell$ | purely reactive |
| $\ell\to\infty$ (lossy) | $Z_{0}$ | $\tanh\gamma\ell\to 1$ |

The last line is worth noting: an infinitely long line looks exactly like $Z_{0}$ — which is the physical meaning of the characteristic impedance, and why a matched load makes a finite line indistinguishable from an infinite one.

\nabla\cdot\mathbf{J}=-\frac{\partial\rho_{v}}{\partial t}
$$

revisionCards.front: Key formulas — Poisson’s & Laplace’s Equations, Capacitance & Uniqueness Theorem
revisionCards.back:
$$
\nabla^{2}V=-\frac{\rho_{v}}{\varepsilon}\quad\text{(Poisson)},\qquad
\nabla^{2}V=0\quad\text{(Laplace, charge-free region)}\\
\nabla^{2}V=\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial x^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial y^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial z^{2}}\\
\nabla^{2}V=\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\!\left(\rho\frac{\partial V}{\partial\rho}\right)+\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\phi^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial z^{2}}\\
\nabla^{2}V=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\!\left(r^{2}\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}\right)
+\frac{1}{r^{2}\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\!\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial V}{\partial\theta}\right)
+\frac{1}{r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}\frac{\partial^{2}V}{\partial\phi^{2}}\\
\nabla^{2}V=-\frac{\rho_{v}}{\varepsilon}\quad\text{(Poisson)},\qquad\nabla^{2}V=0\quad\text{(Laplace)}
$$

revisionCards.front: Key formulas — Curl & Stokes’s Theorem
revisionCards.back:
$$
(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})\cdot\hat{a}_{N}
=\lim_{\Delta S_{N}\to 0}\frac{\oint_{L}\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}}{\Delta S_{N}}\\
\oint_{L}\mathbf{H}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}=\int_{S}(\nabla\times\mathbf{H})\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}\\
(\nabla\times\mathbf{A})_{r}=\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\left(\frac{\partial(A_{\phi}\sin\theta)}{\partial\theta}-\frac{\partial A_{\theta}}{\partial\phi}\right)\\
(\nabla\times\mathbf{A})_{\theta}=\frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial A_{r}}{\partial\phi}-\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(r A_{\phi})}{\partial r}\\
(\nabla\times\mathbf{A})_{\phi}=\frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\partial(r A_{\theta})}{\partial r}-\frac{\partial A_{r}}{\partial\theta}\right)
$$

\mathbf{B}=\nabla\times\mathbf{A}\qquad\text{(valid EVERYWHERE)}\\
\mathbf{A}=\frac{\mu I\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}}{4\pi R}\quad\text{(filament)},\qquad

revisionCards.back:
$$
\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\quad\text{(volts)},\qquad
\mathcal{E} = -N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\quad\text{($N$ turns)},\qquad
\oint_{L}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L} = -\frac{d}{dt}\int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}\\
\Phi = \int_{S}\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}.\\
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}_{s}=-j\omega\mu\mathbf{H}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\times\mathbf{H}_{s}=(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}_{s}=\frac{\rho_{vs}}{\varepsilon},\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{H}_{s}=0.\\
\mathbf{J}_{c}=\sigma\mathbf{E}\quad\text{(conduction)},\qquad
\mathbf{J}_{d}=\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}=\varepsilon\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}\quad\text{(displacement)}.\\
\frac{|\mathbf{J}_{c}|}{|\mathbf{J}_{d}|}=\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}=\frac{\sigma}{2\pi f\varepsilon}=\tan\delta.
$$

revisionCards.front: Key formulas — Maxwell’s Equations
revisionCards.back:
$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{D}=\rho_{v},\qquad\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0\\
\nabla\times\mathbf{E}=-\frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t},\qquad\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{J}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{D}}{\partial t}\\
\oint\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=Q_{\mathrm{enc}},\qquad\oint\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=0\\
\oint\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=-\frac{d}{dt}\int\mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{S},\qquad\oint\mathbf{H}\cdot d\mathbf{L}=I_{\mathrm{enc}}+\frac{d}{dt}\int\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{S}\\
H=\frac{E}{\eta_{0}}=\frac{10}{377}\approx 0.0265\,\mathrm{A/m}
$$

revisionCards.back:
$$
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}=\mu\varepsilon\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^{2}}\quad\text{(lossless, time domain)}\\
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s}=\gamma^{2}\mathbf{E}_{s},\qquad
\nabla^{2}\mathbf{H}_{s}=\gamma^{2}\mathbf{H}_{s}\quad\text{(Helmholtz, phasor form)}\\
\gamma=\alpha+j\beta=\sqrt{j\omega\mu(\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon)}\\
\alpha=\omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\varepsilon}{2}\left(\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^{2}}-1\right)}\quad\text{(Np/m)}\\
\beta=\omega\sqrt{\frac{\mu\varepsilon}{2}\left(\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}\right)^{2}}+1\right)}\quad\text{(rad/m)}
$$

\omega=2\pi\times 10^{8},\qquad\beta=\omega\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}}=\frac{\omega}{c}\sqrt{\varepsilon_{r}}=\frac{2\pi\times 10^{8}}{3\times 10^{8}}\times 2=4.189\,\mathrm{rad/m}\\
v_{p}=\frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_{r}}}=\frac{3\times 10^{8}}{2}=1.5\times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}
$$
